Graded Keller maps and the Jacobian Conjecture

T. Shaska
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We study Keller maps ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} that are equivariant for a linear action of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}, that is homogeneous for an integer grading of the coordinates, and ask what the weight vector alone decides. The sign pattern decides a great deal. If the weights are all of one sign, the setting of weighted projective spaces, a graded Keller map is always an automorphism; in dimension two the same holds for every sign pattern. A graded counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture must therefore have weights of mixed sign and dimension at least three, and the map recently announced as a counterexample, equivariant for wt⁡(x,y,z)=(1,−1,−2)\wt(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-2), realizes the smallest such case. When exactly one weight is positive and equals 11, the Keller condition descends to the invariant quotient, where it says that the Jacobian of the quotient map vanishes along the contracted locus to the order prescribed by the weights. The descended condition is a single equation, multilinear in its arguments, so the graded counterexamples of bounded degree are exactly the rational points of an explicit multiprojective scheme over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and the announced map is one of them. Modulo the natural 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} the parameter space is a weighted projective space with positive weights: a hyperbolic counterexample is parametrised by an elliptic moduli space, of the type in which rational points are governed by a Kummer condition at every prime [11]. We classify graded Keller maps by the signature of the weights, completely in the elliptic and parabolic cases, and reduce the hyperbolic case to that scheme. Over ℚ\mathbb{Q} the image of the announced map is thin, but along the line where the stabilizer is μ2\mu_{2} the Kummer condition of the positive-weight theory reappears.

1. Introduction

A Keller map is a polynomial map ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant, and the Jacobian Conjecture asserts that every such map is a polynomial automorphism. We study Keller maps that are equivariant for a linear action of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}, that is homogeneous for a grading wt⁡(x1,…,xn)=(w1,…,wn)\wt(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=(w_{1},\dots,w_{n}) with wi∈ℤw_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}, and we ask what the weight vector alone decides. The answer is that it decides a great deal, and that the dividing line is the sign pattern. If the weights are all of one sign, the setting of weighted projective spaces, a graded Keller map is always an automorphism (Thm 3.1); in dimension two the same holds for every sign pattern (Thm 3.4). A graded counterexample must therefore have weights of mixed sign and dimension at least three. In that remaining case the Keller condition descends to the invariant quotient, where it becomes a single equation, multilinear in its arguments (Thm 8.3, Thm 9.2), and the counterexamples of bounded degree become the rational points of an explicit scheme over ℤ\mathbb{Z} (Thm 8.9).

Our interest in this question comes from two directions. The first is a recent one. In July 2026, L. Alpöge announced a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension three, credited to the AI system Fable [1]. Define

(1) F:ℂ3→ℂ3(x,y,z)→(a,b,c)\begin{split}F\colon\mathbb{C}^{3}&\to\mathbb{C}^{3}\\ (x,y,z)&\to(a,b,c)\end{split}

where aa, bb, cc are given by the polynomials

(2) a\displaystyle a =(1+x​y)3​z+y2​(1+x​y)​(4+3​x​y),\displaystyle=(1+xy)^{3}z+y^{2}(1+xy)(4+3xy),
b\displaystyle b =y+3​x​(1+x​y)2​z+3​x​y2​(4+3​x​y),\displaystyle=y+3x(1+xy)^{2}z+3xy^{2}(4+3xy),
c\displaystyle c =2​x−3​x2​y−x3​z.\displaystyle=2x-3x^{2}y-x^{3}z.

Denote by detJ​F\det JF the determinant of the Jacobian matrix of FF. We have detJ​F≡−2\det JF\equiv-2, while FF is generically three-to-one. The components of FF are homogeneous for the grading wt⁡(x,y,z)=(1,−1,−2)\wt(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-2), which is hyperbolic and, by the above, the smallest sign pattern and the smallest dimension in which a graded counterexample can occur. The map is the running example of this paper, and in Sec. 8 it becomes a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-point of the parameter scheme just mentioned. Everything we prove about the class is independent of it; the announcement is what makes the class interesting today, not what the results rest on.

That the grading exists was observed independently and earlier in [4, 16], in the opposite sign convention wt⁡(x,y,z)=(−1,1,2)\wt(x,y,z)=(-1,1,2), as were versions of some results of Sec. 4 and Sec. 5; we learned of this after the present analysis was under way, and give independent proofs of everything we use.

The second direction is the one we came from. Graded vector spaces, and the weighted projective spaces attached to them, have been the setting of a series of studies: rational points and heights [11, 2], codes [14], and learning architectures whose layers are graded and whose morphisms are weight-homogeneous [12, 13, 15]. In each the grading is the structure, and the results depend on the weights. The present paper asks the same question for polynomial maps: which properties of a graded polynomial map are already decided by its weight vector? Remark 3.2 records what Thm 3.1 says in the architecture setting.

2. Graded maps

Let 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} be the multiplicative group, that is the affine algebraic group 𝔾m=𝔸1∖{0}\mathbb{G}_{m}=\mathbb{A}^{1}\setminus\{0\} with coordinate ring ℤ⁡[t,t−1]\mathbb{Z}[t,t^{-1}], multiplication as the group operation, and 11 as the identity. Its points are 𝔾m​(ℂ)=ℂ×=ℂ∖{0}\mathbb{G}_{m}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{C}^{\times}=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}, and more generally 𝔾m​(k)=k×\mathbb{G}_{m}(k)=k^{\times} for any field kk.

Let 𝐰=(w1,…,wn)∈ℤn\mathbf{w}=(w_{1},\dots,w_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} be a weight vector. We grade the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] by giving xix_{i} the weight wt⁡(xi)=wi\wt(x_{i})=w_{i}, so that a monomial has weight

wt(x1m1⋯xnmn)=m1w1+⋯+mnwn.\wt\bigl(x_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{m_{n}}\bigr)=m_{1}w_{1}+\dots+m_{n}w_{n}.

A polynomial is called weight-homogeneous of weight ℓ\ell if all its monomials have weight ℓ\ell; the zero polynomial is weight-homogeneous of every weight. We write ℂ​[x]𝐰\mathbb{C}[x]_{\mathbf{w}} for the polynomial ring with this grading, ℂ​[x]𝐰,ℓ\mathbb{C}[x]_{\mathbf{w},\ell} for its piece of weight ℓ\ell, and 𝔸𝐰n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}} for the graded affine space, that is the affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} together with the grading of its coordinate ring. It is 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} equipped with extra structure, not a new variety.

All varieties are over ℂ\mathbb{C} unless stated otherwise, and we write 𝔸n=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{A}^{n}=\Spec\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], so that 𝔸n​(ℂ)=ℂn\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{C}^{n}; the group acting is 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} base changed to ℂ\mathbb{C}. We use 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} when the grading is in play and ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} when the argument is about points, as in the topological step of Thm 3.1. The schemes of Sec. 8 are the exception: they are defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

To any grading 𝐰\mathbf{w} we associate the diagonal action of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} given by

σt​(x1,…,xn)=(tw1​x1,…,twn​xn),t∈𝔾m.\sigma_{t}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\bigl(t^{w_{1}}x_{1},\dots,t^{w_{n}}x_{n}\bigr),\qquad t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}.

Since every algebraic character of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} is t↦tℓt\mapsto t^{\ell} for a unique ℓ∈ℤ\ell\in\mathbb{Z}, the assignment 𝐰↦σ\mathbf{w}\mapsto\sigma is a bijection from ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} onto the set of algebraic 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-actions on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} which are diagonal in the coordinates x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n}, the inverse assignment recovering wiw_{i} as the weight of xix_{i} under σ\sigma. Moreover, for f∈ℂ⁡[x]f\in\mathbb{C}[x] one has f∈ℂ​[x]𝐰,ℓf\in\mathbb{C}[x]_{\mathbf{w},\ell} if and only if f∘σt=tℓ​ff\circ\sigma_{t}=t^{\ell}f for every t∈𝔾mt\in\mathbb{G}_{m}; in particular the weight-zero piece is the ring of invariants,

ℂ​[x]𝐰,0=ℂ​[x]σ.\mathbb{C}[x]_{\mathbf{w},0}=\mathbb{C}[x]^{\sigma}.

We call 𝐰\mathbf{w} elliptic if the wiw_{i} are all nonzero and all of the same sign, parabolic if some wiw_{i} vanishes, and hyperbolic if the wiw_{i} are all nonzero and both signs occur. Every weight vector is of exactly one of these three types, and this trichotomy is the classification proposed in Sec. 11.

Now let 𝐪=(q1,…,qm)∈ℤm\mathbf{q}=(q_{1},\dots,q_{m})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} be a second weight vector, let y1,…,ymy_{1},\dots,y_{m} be the coordinates on the target, and write

τt​(y1,…,ym)=(tq1​y1,…,tqm​ym)\tau_{t}(y_{1},\dots,y_{m})=\bigl(t^{q_{1}}y_{1},\dots,t^{q_{m}}y_{m}\bigr)

for the action associated to 𝐪\mathbf{q}. A polynomial map

(3) G:𝔸𝐰n⟶𝔸𝐪m(x1,…,xn)⟼(G1​(x),…,Gm​(x))\begin{split}G\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}&\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{m}_{\mathbf{q}}\\ (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})&\longmapsto\bigl(G_{1}(x),\ldots,G_{m}(x)\bigr)\end{split}

is called graded if each component GjG_{j} is weight-homogeneous of weight qjq_{j}. We call 𝐰\mathbf{w} the source weights and 𝐪\mathbf{q} the target weights.

Equivalently, GG is graded if and only if it is equivariant, that is,

G∘σt=τt∘G(t∈𝔾m),G\circ\sigma_{t}=\tau_{t}\circ G\qquad(t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}),

or, written out,

G⁡(tw1​x1,…,twn​xn)=(tq1​G1​(x),…,tqm​Gm​(x))(t∈𝔾m),G\bigl(t^{w_{1}}x_{1},\dots,t^{w_{n}}x_{n}\bigr)=\bigl(t^{q_{1}}G_{1}(x),\dots,t^{q_{m}}G_{m}(x)\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}),

which says that the diagram

commutes for every t∈𝔾mt\in\mathbb{G}_{m}. Write

G∗:ℂ⁡[y1,…,ym]⟶ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn],G∗​f=f∘G,G^{*}\colon\mathbb{C}[y_{1},\dots,y_{m}]\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}],\qquad G^{*}f=f\circ G,

for the comorphism of GG, the ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra homomorphism given by composition with GG; thus G∗​yj=GjG^{*}y_{j}=G_{j}. Since weights add under multiplication of polynomials, GG is graded if and only if G∗G^{*} preserves weights, that is,

G∗​(ℂ​[y]𝐪,ℓ)⊆ℂ​[x]𝐰,ℓfor every ​ℓ∈ℤ,G^{*}\bigl(\mathbb{C}[y]_{\mathbf{q},\ell}\bigr)\subseteq\mathbb{C}[x]_{\mathbf{w},\ell}\qquad\text{for every }\ell\in\mathbb{Z},

so that G∗G^{*} is a homomorphism of graded rings of degree 00.

Graded affine spaces and graded maps form a category: it is the full subcategory of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-varieties whose objects are affine spaces with a diagonal linear action, and under G↦G∗G\mapsto G^{*} it is anti-equivalent to the corresponding category of graded polynomial algebras and degree-zero homomorphisms. In particular id\id is graded, and G∘HG\circ H is graded whenever GG and HH are, since (G∘H)∗=H∗∘G∗(G\circ H)^{*}=H^{*}\circ G^{*}. We write Aut𝐰⁡(𝔸n)\Aut_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbb{A}^{n}) for the group of graded automorphisms of 𝔸𝐰n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}, that is the polynomial automorphisms of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} commuting with σ\sigma; it is the group from which the liftable automorphisms of Sec. 8 are obtained.

Two graded affine spaces 𝔸𝐰n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}} and 𝔸𝐪n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}} are carried to one another by a permutation of coordinates exactly when 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a permutation of 𝐰\mathbf{w}.

Let g=gcd⁡(w1,…,wn,q1,…,qm)g=\gcd(w_{1},\dots,w_{n},q_{1},\dots,q_{m}), and assume that 𝐰\mathbf{w} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} are not both zero, so that g≥1g\geq 1. The subgroup of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} acting trivially on both 𝔸𝐰n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}} and 𝔸𝐪m\mathbb{A}^{m}_{\mathbf{q}} is

ker⁡σ∩ker⁡τ=μg.\ker\sigma\cap\ker\tau=\mu_{g}.

Both actions therefore factor through 𝔾m/μg\mathbb{G}_{m}/\mu_{g}, and the isomorphism 𝔾m/μg≅𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}/\mu_{g}\cong\mathbb{G}_{m} induced by t↦tgt\mapsto t^{g} carries them to the actions associated to 𝐰/g\mathbf{w}/g and 𝐪/g\mathbf{q}/g. Since gg divides every wiw_{i} and every qjq_{j}, the pieces of weight not divisible by gg are zero, while

ℂ​[x]𝐰,g​ℓ=ℂ​[x]𝐰/g,ℓandℂ​[y]𝐪,g​ℓ=ℂ​[y]𝐪/g,ℓ\mathbb{C}[x]_{\mathbf{w},g\ell}=\mathbb{C}[x]_{\mathbf{w}/g,\ell}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{C}[y]_{\mathbf{q},g\ell}=\mathbb{C}[y]_{\mathbf{q}/g,\ell}

for every ℓ∈ℤ\ell\in\mathbb{Z}. The two pairs of weight vectors thus give the same decompositions, up to reindexing, and define the same graded maps.

For the remainder of this section we take m=nm=n, so that the Jacobian matrix J​GJG is square. By detJ​G\det JG we denote its determinant.

Lemma 2.1.

Let GG be as in Eq. 3. The following hold:

i) detJ​G\det JG is weight-homogeneous of weight

wt⁡(detJ​G)=∑qj−∑wi.\wt(\det JG)=\sum q_{j}-\sum w_{i}.

Moreover, if detJ​G\det JG is a nonzero constant, then ∑qj=∑wi\sum q_{j}=\sum w_{i}.

ii) If qj≠0q_{j}\neq 0 then Gj​(0)=0G_{j}(0)=0; in particular G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0 as soon as all qjq_{j} are nonzero.

iii) For all ii and jj,

∂Gj∂xi​(0)=0\frac{\partial G_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}(0)=0

unless qj=wiq_{j}=w_{i}.

Proof.

Differentiating the equivariance in xx gives

J​G​(σt​p)​diag⁡(tw1,…,twn)=diag⁡(tq1,…,tqn)​J​G​(p),JG(\sigma_{t}p)\,\diag(t^{w_{1}},\dots,t^{w_{n}})=\diag(t^{q_{1}},\dots,t^{q_{n}})\,JG(p),

and hence

detJ​G​(σt​p)=t∑qj−∑wi​detJ​G​(p),\det JG(\sigma_{t}p)=t^{\sum q_{j}-\sum w_{i}}\det JG(p),

which proves i), the second assertion because a nonzero constant has weight 00.

Setting x=0x=0 in the equivariance gives

tqj​Gj​(0)=Gj​(0)t^{q_{j}}G_{j}(0)=G_{j}(0)

for all tt; since qj≠0q_{j}\neq 0, this forces Gj​(0)=0G_{j}(0)=0, which is ii). Finally, the entry ∂Gj/∂xi\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{i} is weight-homogeneous of weight qj−wiq_{j}-w_{i}, and 00 is a fixed point of σ\sigma, so evaluating the corresponding scaling identity there gives

∂Gj/∂xi​(0)=tqj−wi​∂Gj/∂xi​(0)\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{i}(0)=t^{\,q_{j}-w_{i}}\,\partial G_{j}/\partial x_{i}(0)

for all tt, which forces the entry to vanish unless qj=wiq_{j}=w_{i}. This is iii), and no hypothesis on the weights is used. ∎

Lemma 2.2.

Let GG be as in Eq. 3, with detJ​G​(0)≠0\det JG(0)\neq 0. Then there is a permutation π\pi of {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} with qj=wπ⁡(j)q_{j}=w_{\pi(j)} for all jj; if the wiw_{i} are pairwise distinct, π\pi is unique and J​G​(0)JG(0) is supported on the graph of π\pi.

Proof.

Expand

detJ​G​(0)=∑πsgn⁡(π)​∏j∂Gj∂xπ⁡(j)​(0).\det JG(0)=\sum_{\pi}\sgn(\pi)\prod_{j}\frac{\partial G_{j}}{\partial x_{\pi(j)}}(0).

By part iii) of Lem 2.1 each factor vanishes unless qj=wπ⁡(j)q_{j}=w_{\pi(j)}, so a nonzero determinant requires at least one permutation along which all the equalities hold. If the wiw_{i} are distinct, the condition qj=wπ⁡(j)q_{j}=w_{\pi(j)} determines π⁡(j)\pi(j), and every other entry of J​G​(0)JG(0) vanishes. ∎

A polynomial map G:ℂn→ℂnG\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is called a Keller map if detJ​G\det JG is a nonzero constant, and a polynomial automorphism if it is bijective with polynomial inverse. The Jacobian Conjecture asserts that every Keller map is a polynomial automorphism. We call GG a graded Keller map if in addition it is graded for some pair of weight vectors 𝐰,𝐪\mathbf{w},\mathbf{q}.

Corollary 2.3.

Let GG be a graded Keller map with source weights 𝐰\mathbf{w} and target weights 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Then 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a permutation of 𝐰\mathbf{w}. Consequently:

  1. i)

    ∑qj=∑wi\sum q_{j}=\sum w_{i};

  2. ii)

    a permutation of the coordinates is a graded isomorphism 𝔸𝐰n→𝔸𝐪n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}};

  3. iii)

    𝐰\mathbf{w} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} are of the same type, elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic;

  4. iv)

    gcd⁡(q1,…,qn)=gcd⁡(w1,…,wn)\gcd(q_{1},\dots,q_{n})=\gcd(w_{1},\dots,w_{n}), so the normalisation g=1g=1 says exactly that gcd⁡(w1,…,wn)=1\gcd(w_{1},\dots,w_{n})=1.

Proof.

Since detJ​G\det JG is a nonzero constant we have detJ​G​(0)=detJ​G≠0\det JG(0)=\det JG\neq 0, so Lem 2.2 provides a permutation π\pi with qj=wπ⁡(j)q_{j}=w_{\pi(j)} for all jj; that is, (q1,…,qn)(q_{1},\dots,q_{n}) is a rearrangement of (w1,…,wn)(w_{1},\dots,w_{n}). Now i) holds because equal multisets have equal sums, refining Lem 2.1(i), and ii) is the criterion for a permutation of coordinates to be graded, recorded above.

For iii) and iv), the type of a weight vector depends only on the signs of its entries and the gcd\gcd only on their values, neither being affected by the ordering and

g=gcd⁡(gcd⁡(w1,…,wn),gcd⁡(q1,…,qn))=gcd⁡(w1,…,wn).g=\gcd\bigl(\gcd(w_{1},\dots,w_{n}),\,\gcd(q_{1},\dots,q_{n})\bigr)=\gcd(w_{1},\dots,w_{n}).

∎

2.1. A counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture

We now specialize to the map F:ℂ3→ℂ3F\colon\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} of Eq. 1. Take n=3n=3, source weights 𝐰=(1,−1,−2)\mathbf{w}=(1,-1,-2) on ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] and target weights 𝐪=(−2,−1,1)\mathbf{q}=(-2,-1,1) on ℂ⁡[a,b,c]\mathbb{C}[a,b,c], so that

wt⁡(xi​yj​zℓ)=i−j−2​ℓ,\wt(x^{i}y^{j}z^{\ell})=i-j-2\ell,

and x​yxy and x2​zx^{2}z have weight 00. Each component of FF is weight-homogeneous, with wt⁡(a)=−2\wt(a)=-2, wt⁡(b)=−1\wt(b)=-1, wt⁡(c)=1\wt(c)=1, so FF is graded, and by the above this is the same as

(4) F∘σt=τt∘F(t∈𝔾m),F\circ\sigma_{t}=\tau_{t}\circ F\qquad(t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}),

where

σt​(x,y,z)=(t​x,t−1​y,t−2​z)τt​(a,b,c)=(t−2​a,t−1​b,t​c).\sigma_{t}(x,y,z)=\bigl(tx,\,t^{-1}y,\,t^{-2}z\bigr)\qquad\tau_{t}(a,b,c)=\bigl(t^{-2}a,\,t^{-1}b,\,tc\bigr).

Both weight vectors are hyperbolic. The grading is unique up to scaling: weight-homogeneity of the three monomials of cc alone forces w2=−w1w_{2}=-w_{1} and w3=−2​w1w_{3}=-2w_{1}, so 𝐰\mathbf{w} is a multiple of (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2) and is an invariant of the map.

The target weight vector (−2,−1,1)(-2,-1,1) is the reversal of the source weight vector (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2), so

∑qj=∑wi=−2,\sum q_{j}=\sum w_{i}=-2,

and the weights are distinct, so by Lem 2.2 the permutation π\pi is the reversal and, by Lem 2.1(iii), the linear part of FF at the origin is anti-diagonal:

∂a∂z=1,∂b∂y=1,∂c∂x=2.\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}=1,\quad\frac{\partial b}{\partial y}=1,\quad\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}=2.

Since detJ​F\det JF is constant it equals detJ​F​(0)\det JF(0), and since the reversal permutation on three letters is odd,

detJ​F=detJ​F​(0)=−(1⋅1⋅2)=−2.\det JF\;=\;\det JF(0)\;=\;-(1\cdot 1\cdot 2)\;=\;-2.

The constant −2-2 is the product of the three anti-diagonal leading coefficients.

3. Two cases of the Jacobian Conjecture

In two cases a graded Keller map is a polynomial automorphism for a reason visible in the weights alone: elliptic weights in every dimension, where the orbits give properness, and dimension two for every signature, where the invariant ring is generated by one element and a degree count closes the argument. What remains is the hyperbolic case in dimension three and above, and Eq. 1 is an instance of it.

3.1. The elliptic case in any dimension

Theorem 3.1.

Let G:𝔸𝐰n→𝔸𝐪nG\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}} be a graded Keller map with elliptic weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}. Then GG is an isomorphism of graded affine spaces: it is bijective, its inverse is polynomial, and G−1:𝔸𝐪n→𝔸𝐰nG^{-1}\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}} is graded. Forgetting the gradings, GG is a polynomial automorphism of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}.

Proof.

By Cor 2.3 the target weights 𝐪\mathbf{q} are a permutation of 𝐰\mathbf{w}, hence also elliptic and of the same sign. If all the weights are negative, replacing tt by t−1t^{-1} in both actions replaces (𝐰,𝐪)(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{q}) by (−𝐰,−𝐪)(-\mathbf{w},-\mathbf{q}) and changes neither the map nor its being graded; so we may assume wi>0w_{i}>0 for all ii, and then qj>0q_{j}>0 for all jj.

Since detJ​G\det JG is a nonzero constant, GG is étale. Steps 1–3 argue on complex points, so we write x,y,px,y,p for points of 𝔸n​(ℂ)=ℂn\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{C}^{n} and use the Euclidean topology throughout; there GG is a local biholomorphism.

Step 1: G−1​(0)={0}G^{-1}(0)=\{0\}. The weights qjq_{j} are nonzero, so G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0 by Lem 2.1(ii). Suppose G⁡(p)=0G(p)=0 with p≠0p\neq 0. The orbit map t↦σt​(p)t\mapsto\sigma_{t}(p) is non-constant: σt​(p)=p\sigma_{t}(p)=p for all tt would force twi​pi=pit^{w_{i}}p_{i}=p_{i} for all tt and all ii, hence p=0p=0 as all wi>0w_{i}>0. But

G⁡(σt​p)=τt​G​(p)=τt​(0)=0,G(\sigma_{t}p)=\tau_{t}G(p)=\tau_{t}(0)=0,

so the infinite connected set {σt​(p):t∈ℂ×}\{\sigma_{t}(p):t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}\} lies in G−1​(0)G^{-1}(0), which is discrete because GG is étale — a contradiction.

Step 2: GG is proper. Define

ρ⁡(x)=maxi⁡|xi|1/wi and ρ′​(y)=maxj⁡|yj|1/qj,\rho(x)=\max_{i}|x_{i}|^{1/w_{i}}\quad\text{ and }\quad\rho^{\prime}(y)=\max_{j}|y_{j}|^{1/q_{j}},

which make sense because all wiw_{i} and all qjq_{j} are positive. Both are continuous and vanish only at the origin. For t∈ℝ>0t\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} we have

ρ⁡(σt​x)=t​ρ​(x) and ρ′​(τt​y)=t​ρ′​(y).\rho(\sigma_{t}x)=t\rho(x)\quad\text{ and }\quad\rho^{\prime}(\tau_{t}y)=t\rho^{\prime}(y).

The slice S={ρ=1}S=\{\rho=1\} is closed and bounded, hence compact, and every p≠0p\neq 0 is σt​(p¯)\sigma_{t}(\bar{p}) with t=ρ⁡(p)t=\rho(p) and p¯=σ1/t​(p)∈S\bar{p}=\sigma_{1/t}(p)\in S. By Step 1, 0∉G⁡(S)0\notin G(S), so

δ:=miny∈G⁡(S)⁡ρ′​(y)>0\delta:=\min_{y\in G(S)}\rho^{\prime}(y)>0

by compactness of G⁡(S)G(S). Let K⊆ℂnK\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n} be compact and suppose pk∈G−1​(K)p_{k}\in G^{-1}(K) with |pk|→∞|p_{k}|\to\infty, so tk:=ρ⁡(pk)→∞t_{k}:=\rho(p_{k})\to\infty. Then

ρ′​(G⁡(pk))=ρ′​(τtk​G​(p¯k))=tk​ρ′​(G⁡(p¯k))≥tk​δ⟶∞,\rho^{\prime}\bigl(G(p_{k})\bigr)=\rho^{\prime}\bigl(\tau_{t_{k}}G(\bar{p}_{k})\bigr)=t_{k}\,\rho^{\prime}\bigl(G(\bar{p}_{k})\bigr)\ \geq\ t_{k}\,\delta\ \longrightarrow\ \infty,

contradicting G⁡(pk)∈KG(p_{k})\in K. Hence G−1​(K)G^{-1}(K) is bounded, and it is closed since GG is continuous, so it is compact and GG is proper.

Step 3: conclusion. A proper local homeomorphism onto a connected, locally compact Hausdorff space is a covering map with finite fibers; hence GG is a finite covering of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} by ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. The base is simply connected, so the covering is trivial; the total space is connected, so it has one sheet, and GG is bijective. An injective polynomial map ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is a polynomial automorphism [9], so G−1G^{-1} is polynomial. Applying G−1G^{-1} on both sides of G∘σt=τt∘GG\circ\sigma_{t}=\tau_{t}\circ G gives

G−1∘τt=σt∘G−1(t∈𝔾m),G^{-1}\circ\tau_{t}=\sigma_{t}\circ G^{-1}\qquad(t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}),

so G−1G^{-1} is graded with source weights 𝐪\mathbf{q} and target weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}. ∎

Remark 3.2.

Theorem 3.1 has a reading outside algebraic geometry. In the graded architectures of [13, 12, 15], the data carried by a node is a graded vector space and the admissible maps are those respecting the grading, so that the symmetry group of a layer is the group Aut𝐰⁡(𝔸n)\Aut_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbb{A}^{n}) of Sec. 2. For a polynomial layer map of elliptic weight type, Thm 3.1 says that a nonzero constant Jacobian determinant already forces bijectivity, with polynomial inverse, and the inverse is again graded with the same weights. Constancy of detJ​G\det JG is the condition one imposes in any case when the log-determinant is to be tractable; in the positive-weight setting invertibility is not an extra hypothesis but a consequence of it. No such statement is available without a grading, where it is the Jacobian Conjecture itself. Theorem 3.4 extends it to every signature in dimension two, and the rest of this paper shows that both statements are sharp: the map Eq. 1 is graded for the mixed-sign weights (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2), has constant Jacobian determinant, and is three-to-one. What separates the two behaviours is the signature of the grading and nothing else.

Elliptic weights are the setting of weighted projective spaces and of the Veronese morphisms between them; Thm 3.1 says the Jacobian Conjecture is trivially true there for graded maps. A graded counterexample is therefore forced into parabolic or hyperbolic weights, and by Thm 3.4 into dimension at least three; the weights (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2) of Eq. 1 are the smallest for which we know an example to exist.

Remark 3.3.

Hyperbolic weights are necessary but not sufficient. Let G=X+HG=X+H on ℂ5\mathbb{C}^{5}, where

H=(0,X1​X3,X1​X4+12​X22,X1​X5−X2​X3,12​X32)H=\bigl(0,\;X_{1}X_{3},\;X_{1}X_{4}+\tfrac{1}{2}X_{2}^{2},\;X_{1}X_{5}-X_{2}X_{3},\;\tfrac{1}{2}X_{3}^{2}\bigr)

is the map of Vasyunin, reported in [7]. Weight-homogeneity of the four nonlinear components forces 𝐰=𝐪=(1,−1,−2,−3,−4)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{q}=(1,-1,-2,-3,-4), so GG is graded with hyperbolic weights, and J​HJH is nilpotent, so detJ​G=1\det JG=1 and GG is a Keller map. It is an automorphism, since deg⁡G=2\deg G=2 [17], but it is not linearly triangularizable [7], and it is the extremal example for the strong nilpotence results of [8]. The examples of [8, §4] in every dimension are graded in the same way, with hyperbolic or parabolic weights, never elliptic. We return to this map in Rem 8.8.

3.2. Dimension two, all signatures

In dimension two there is no graded counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, for any weight vector. We prove more: every Keller map of the plane admitting a nontrivial 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-equivariance is, after a change of coordinates on source and target, one of three normal forms, listed by the type of the weights.

Theorem 3.4.

Let G:𝔸2→𝔸2G\colon\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{2} be a Keller map. Let θ\theta and η\eta be algebraic actions of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} on the source and on the target copy of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}, neither assumed diagonal in the given coordinates, with θ\theta nontrivial, and suppose

G∘θt=ηt∘G(t∈𝔾m).G\circ\theta_{t}=\eta_{t}\circ G\qquad(t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}).

Then GG is a polynomial automorphism. More precisely, there are polynomial automorphisms φ,ψ\varphi,\psi of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} such that φ\varphi carries θ\theta and ψ\psi carries η\eta to diagonal actions σ\sigma and τ\tau, with source weights 𝐰=(w1,w2)\mathbf{w}=(w_{1},w_{2}), and ψ∘G∘φ−1\psi\circ G\circ\varphi^{-1} is:

  1. (1)

    triangular if 𝐰\mathbf{w} is elliptic, and linear if moreover w1=w2w_{1}=w_{2};

  2. (2)

    affine, if 𝐰\mathbf{w} is parabolic;

  3. (3)

    linear, of the form (x,y)↦(a0​x,b0​y)(x,y)\mapsto(a_{0}x,b_{0}y) or (x,y)↦(a0​y,b0​x)(x,y)\mapsto(a_{0}y,b_{0}x), if 𝐰\mathbf{w} is hyperbolic.

Proof.

The actions θ\theta and η\eta are not assumed diagonal, so no weight vector is attached to them at the outset; the weight vectors of Sec. 2 appear only after linearization. Every algebraic 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action on 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} is linearizable by a polynomial automorphism [5], and a linear action is diagonalizable, every rational representation of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} being a sum of characters; so we may choose φ,ψ\varphi,\psi for which

σt=φ∘θt∘φ−1andτt=ψ∘ηt∘ψ−1\sigma_{t}=\varphi\circ\theta_{t}\circ\varphi^{-1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tau_{t}=\psi\circ\eta_{t}\circ\psi^{-1}

are diagonal. Put G′:=ψ∘G∘φ−1G^{\prime}:=\psi\circ G\circ\varphi^{-1}. Then

G′∘σt=ψ∘G∘θt∘φ−1=ψ∘ηt∘G∘φ−1=τt∘G′,G^{\prime}\circ\sigma_{t}=\psi\circ G\circ\theta_{t}\circ\varphi^{-1}=\psi\circ\eta_{t}\circ G\circ\varphi^{-1}=\tau_{t}\circ G^{\prime},

so G′G^{\prime} is graded in the sense of Sec. 2 for the weight vectors of σ\sigma and τ\tau. Since a polynomial automorphism has constant nonzero Jacobian, G′G^{\prime} is again a Keller map, and GG is a polynomial automorphism if and only if G′G^{\prime} is. We may therefore assume from the outset that GG is graded, with source weights 𝐰=(w1,w2)\mathbf{w}=(w_{1},w_{2}) and target weights 𝐪=(q1,q2)\mathbf{q}=(q_{1},q_{2}); and we remain free to compose with a permutation of the source coordinates, absorbing it into φ\varphi, and with a permutation of the target coordinates, absorbing it into ψ\psi.

By Cor 2.3 the vector 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a permutation of 𝐰\mathbf{w}, so composing with a permutation of the target coordinates we may assume 𝐪=𝐰\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{w}; in the hyperbolic case the alternative 𝐪=(w2,w1)\mathbf{q}=(w_{2},w_{1}) leads in the same way to the second normal form in (3), and we return to it at the end. Replacing tt by t−1t^{-1} in both actions replaces 𝐰\mathbf{w} by −𝐰-\mathbf{w} and changes neither GG nor its being graded, so we may fix the sign of w1w_{1} as convenient. Since θ\theta is nontrivial so is σ\sigma, and therefore 𝐰≠(0,0)\mathbf{w}\neq(0,0).

The elliptic case. Here the wiw_{i} are nonzero and of one sign; after the substitution above we may take them positive, and after a permutation of the source coordinates that 0<w1≤w20<w_{1}\leq w_{2}. The weight-ℓ\ell piece of ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] is spanned by the monomials xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} with i​w1+j​w2=ℓiw_{1}+jw_{2}=\ell, and since both weights are positive only finitely many (i,j)(i,j) occur.

Suppose first w1<w2w_{1}<w_{2}. A monomial of weight w1w_{1} has j=0j=0, since j≥1j\geq 1 would give i​w1+j​w2≥w2>w1iw_{1}+jw_{2}\geq w_{2}>w_{1}, and then i=1i=1; so the weight-w1w_{1} piece is ℂ​x\mathbb{C}x. A monomial of weight w2w_{2} has j≤1j\leq 1; if j=1j=1 then i=0i=0, and if j=0j=0 then i​w1=w2iw_{1}=w_{2}, which is solvable only when w1w_{1} divides w2w_{2}. Hence the weight-w2w_{2} piece is ℂ​y\mathbb{C}y, together with ℂ​xw2/w1\mathbb{C}x^{w_{2}/w_{1}} in that case. Therefore

G=(a0​x,b0​y+b1​xw2/w1),detJ​G=a0​b0,G=\bigl(a_{0}x,\;b_{0}y+b_{1}x^{w_{2}/w_{1}}\bigr),\qquad\det JG=a_{0}b_{0},

The Keller condition says a0​b0≠0a_{0}b_{0}\neq 0, so GG is triangular with nonzero diagonal, hence a polynomial automorphism. If instead w1=w2w_{1}=w_{2}, then i​w1+j​w2=w1iw_{1}+jw_{2}=w_{1} forces i+j=1i+j=1, so both pieces equal ℂ​x+ℂ​y\mathbb{C}x+\mathbb{C}y and GG is linear, with invertible matrix because detJ​G≠0\det JG\neq 0.

The parabolic case. Some wiw_{i} vanishes, and not both, so after a permutation of the source coordinates 𝐰=(w1,0)\mathbf{w}=(w_{1},0) with w1≠0w_{1}\neq 0, and after the substitution above w1>0w_{1}>0. The hyperbolic case. The wiw_{i} are nonzero of opposite signs, so after a permutation of the source coordinates and the substitution above 𝐰=(p,−q)\mathbf{w}=(p,-q) with p,q>0p,q>0; and after the reduction by g=gcdg=\gcd of Sec. 2, which does not change the graded maps, we may assume gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1. ℂ​[x,y]σ=ℂ⁡[u],u=xq​yp,\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{\sigma}=\mathbb{C}[u],\qquad u=x^{q}y^{p},

In the elliptic and parabolic cases the resulting normal forms are again triangular and affine respectively, and in the hyperbolic case one obtains (x,y)↦(a0​y,b0​x)(x,y)\mapsto(a_{0}y,b_{0}x), the second form in (3). 4. Descent and the fiber cubic

Sec. 2 and Sec. 3 concerned graded Keller maps in general. We now turn to the single map Eq. 1 and study it for the next three sections. The organizing fact is that the grading reduces its fibres to the roots of one cubic in one variable, with coefficients in the invariants of the target action; everything we prove about Eq. 1 is read off that cubic.

The invariant rings of the two actions are polynomial:

ℂ​[x,y,z]σ=ℂ⁡[u,v],u=x​y,v=x2​z;ℂ​[a,b,c]τ=ℂ⁡[P,Q],P=b​c,Q=a​c2.\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]^{\sigma}=\mathbb{C}[u,v],\quad u=xy,\;v=x^{2}z;\qquad\mathbb{C}[a,b,c]^{\tau}=\mathbb{C}[P,Q],\quad P=bc,\;Q=ac^{2}.

Generic orbits are free and closed, and by Eq. 4 the map FF carries orbits bijectively to orbits, so FF descends to F¯:𝔸u,v2→𝔸P,Q2\overline{F}\colon\mathbb{A}^{2}_{u,v}\to\mathbb{A}^{2}_{P,Q}. Set

L=2−3​u−v,M=v​(1+u)2+u2​(4+3​u),L=2-3u-v,\qquad M=v(1+u)^{2}+u^{2}(4+3u),

so that c=x​Lc=xL and, directly from Eq. 1,

(5) P=L⁡(u+3​M),Q=L2​(1+u)​M.P=L\,(u+3M),\qquad Q=L^{2}(1+u)\,M.

Substituting v=2−3​u−Lv=2-3u-L into MM, the cubic terms cancel identically:

(6) M=(2+u)−L​(1+u)2.M=(2+u)-L(1+u)^{2}.

    L=12​(P−4​s+3​s2),e=s/L,u=e−1,v=2−3​u−L,L=\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(P-4s+3s^{2}\right),\quad e=s/L,\quad u=e-1,\quad v=2-3u-L,

Lemma 4.2.

Let E/FE/F be a finite field extension and TT transcendental over EE. Then [E(T):F(T)]=[E:F][E(T):F(T)]=[E:F].

Proof.

A basis e1,…,ene_{1},\dots,e_{n} of E/FE/F spans E⁡[T]E[T] over F⁡[T]F[T], hence E⁡(T)E(T) over F⁡(T)F(T). If

∑ifi​(T)​ei=0\sum_{i}f_{i}(T)\,e_{i}=0

with fi∈F⁡[T]f_{i}\in F[T] not all zero, then comparing coefficients of each power of TT gives FF-linear relations among the eie_{i}, forcing every coefficient of every fif_{i} to vanish. So the eie_{i} remain independent over F⁡(T)F(T). ∎

Proposition 4.3.

Write Ω=ℂ⁡(x,y,z)\Omega=\mathbb{C}(x,y,z) and let K=ℂ⁡(a,b,c)⊆ΩK=\mathbb{C}(a,b,c)\subseteq\Omega be the subfield generated by the components of FF. Then:

  1. (1)

    a,b,ca,b,c are algebraically independent over ℂ\mathbb{C}, so KK is rational of transcendence degree 33;

  2. (2)

    [Ω:K]=3[\Omega:K]=3;

  3. (3)

    the cubic Eq. 7 is irreducible over KK, hence also over its subfield ℂ⁡(P,Q)\mathbb{C}(P,Q), and is the minimal polynomial of ss over both.

In particular the generic fiber of FF has exactly three points, independently of the announcement.

Proof.

(1) In characteristic zero, a,b,c∈ℂ⁡(x,y,z)a,b,c\in\mathbb{C}(x,y,z) are algebraically independent if and only if

det(∂(a,b,c)/∂(x,y,z))≠0\det\bigl(\partial(a,b,c)/\partial(x,y,z)\bigr)\neq 0

where the determinant is −2-2.

(2) We first identify the invariant subfields. On {x≠0}\{x\neq 0\} the action σ\sigma is free, and each orbit meets the slice {x=1}\{x=1\} exactly once, at

The cubic Eq. 7 makes the failure of properness visible: as a target point moves onto the discriminant, no two preimages ever meet. We now make this precise.

Remark 5.3 (A Kummer condition on the stacky line).

The action τ\tau has stabilizer μ2\mu_{2} exactly along the punctured line {b=c=0,a≠0}\{b=c=0,\ a\neq 0\}, and σ\sigma has stabilizer μ2\mu_{2} along {x=y=0,z≠0}\{x=y=0,\ z\neq 0\}. By Prop 5.2, for α∈ℚ×\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times} the two preimages of (α,0,0)(\alpha,0,0) lying on {L=0}\{L=0\} have x2=−14​αx^{2}=-\tfrac{1}{4\alpha}, so

#​F−1​(α,0,0)​(ℚ)={3,−α∈(ℚ×)2,1,otherwise,\#F^{-1}(\alpha,0,0)(\mathbb{Q})=\begin{cases}3,&-\alpha\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{2},\\ 1,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}

the point (0,0,α)(0,0,\alpha) occurring in either case. Liftability of a rational point along the μ2\mu_{2}-fixed line is thus governed by a square class, an obstruction of exactly the Kummer type that governs the positive-weight setting [11]. The announced collision is the member α=−14\alpha=-\tfrac{1}{4} of this family, and α=−1\alpha=-1, with preimages (±12,∓3,26)(\pm\tfrac{1}{2},\mp 3,26), is the next.

Remark 5.4.

The three roots of Eq. 7 always sum to 2=|detJ​F|2=|\det JF|, the same constant produced by the anti-diagonal linear part in Lem 2.1; equivalently, the coefficient of s2s^{2} is −2-2. This is a statement about the roots and not about the fiber: on the discriminant the double root s0s_{0} has L⁡(s0)=0L(s_{0})=0 and is not a preimage, so the surviving point carries s=2−2​s0s=2-2s_{0}, which equals 22 only when s0=0s_{0}=0. The same constant appears once more as the value κ=2\kappa=2 of Thm 8.3. Whether the s2s^{2}-coefficient of the fiber cubic equals κ\kappa for every Keller map graded by this weight type, or whether these coincidences are accidents of Eq. 1, we do not know.

6. Arithmetic: the image on rational points is thin

Everything above is defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. If (x,y,z)∈ℚ3(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3}, then s=L​e∈ℚs=Le\in\mathbb{Q}; hence a point (a,b,c)∈ℚ3(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3} with c≠0c\neq 0 has a rational preimage if and only if the cubic Eq. 7 has a rational root with L≠0L\neq 0.

Corollary 6.1.

F⁡(ℚ3)F(\mathbb{Q}^{3}) is a thin set in the sense of Serre [10]. By Hilbert irreducibility, outside a thin set of rational points (a,b,c)∈ℚ3(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3} the fiber F−1​(a,b,c)F^{-1}(a,b,c) contains no rational point.

Proof.

The source ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} is irreducible and FF is dominant of degree 33 by Prop 4.3, so F⁡(ℚ3)F(\mathbb{Q}^{3}) is the image of the rational points of an irreducible variety under a generically finite map of degree greater than one; such images are thin by definition [10, §3.1]. The second statement is Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem applied to the cubic Eq. 7, which is irreducible over ℂ⁡(a,b,c)\mathbb{C}(a,b,c) by Prop 4.3(3). ∎

Over ℂ\mathbb{C} almost every point of the target has three preimages; over ℚ\mathbb{Q} almost none has any. The counterexample therefore fails bijectivity on ℚ\mathbb{Q}-points in both directions at once: rational collisions, and a thin image. It is instructive to compare with the lifting problem for the Veronese morphism φ:𝕎​ℙ𝐪n→ℙn\varphi\colon\mathbb{WP}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}}\to\mathbb{P}^{n} on weighted projective spaces [11]. There the weights are positive, φ\varphi is finite and ramified, and liftability of a rational point is an abelian condition: a torsor under roots of unity, classified by Kummer classes and detected by congruences at every prime. Here the weights are hyperbolic, FF is étale and non-proper, and liftability is the splitting of a nonabelian S3S_{3}-resolvent, with no torsor structure and no congruence criterion — except along the stabilizer locus, where Rem 5.3 shows the abelian condition returns.

7. Descent of the Keller condition

The identity detJ​F=−2\det JF=-2 is equivalent to a two-dimensional statement about F¯\overline{F} and the contracted line. The following holds for every equivariant map of this weight type, not only for Eq. 1.

Theorem 7.1.

Let G:ℂ3→ℂ3G\colon\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} be a dominant polynomial map equivariant for σ,τ\sigma,\tau as in Eq. 4, with weights (1,−1,−2)(1,-1,-2) and degrees (−2,−1,1)(-2,-1,1). Write the third component as G3=x​Λ​(u,v)G_{3}=x\,\Lambda(u,v) with Λ\Lambda invariant, and let (P,Q)=(G2​G3,G1​G32)(P,Q)=(G_{2}G_{3},\,G_{1}G_{3}^{2}) be the descended map on invariants. Then, up to a universal sign,

detJ​G=±Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)Λ2.\det JG\;=\;\pm\,\frac{\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)}{\Lambda^{2}}\,.

Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=κ​Λ2for some ​κ∈ℂ×,\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)\;=\;\kappa\,\Lambda^{2}\qquad\text{for some }\kappa\in\mathbb{C}^{\times},

that is, if and only if the Jacobian of the quotient map vanishes exactly on the contracted locus {Λ=0}\{\Lambda=0\}, to order two, with constant leading coefficient. For the map Eq. 1 we have Λ=L\Lambda=L and Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=2​L2.\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=2L^{2}.

The component G3G_{3} has weight 11, and every weight-one rational function on {x≠0}\{x\neq 0\} is xx times an invariant, so G3=x​ΛG_{3}=x\Lambda with Λ∈ℂ⁡[u,v]\Lambda\in\mathbb{C}[u,v]; likewise P,QP,Q are invariant. On {x≠0}\{x\neq 0\} use coordinates (x,u,v)(x,u,v), and on {G3≠0}\{G_{3}\neq 0\} target coordinates (c,P,Q)(c,P,Q), related to (a,b,c)(a,b,c) by a=Q/c2a=Q/c^{2}, b=P/cb=P/c. In these coordinates GG is

(x,u,v)↦(x​Λ​(u,v),P⁡(u,v),Q⁡(u,v)),(x,u,v)\mapsto\bigl(x\Lambda(u,v),\,P(u,v),\,Q(u,v)\bigr),

with Jacobian Λ⋅Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)\Lambda\cdot\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q). The source change (x,y,z)→(x,u,v)(x,y,z)\to(x,u,v) has Jacobian ±x3\pm x^{3} and the target change (c,P,Q)→(a,b,c)(c,P,Q)\to(a,b,c) has Jacobian ±c−3=±(x​Λ)−3\pm c^{-3}=\pm(x\Lambda)^{-3}, whence

detJ​G=±x3​(x​Λ)−3​Λ​Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=±Λ−2​Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)\det JG=\pm\,x^{3}\,(x\Lambda)^{-3}\,\Lambda\,\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=\pm\,\Lambda^{-2}\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)

on a dense open set, hence everywhere. The displayed value for Eq. 1 is a direct computation through the coordinates of Lem 4.1: one finds

∂(P,Q)∂(s,L)=−2​L,∂(s,L)∂(e,L)=L,∂(e,L)∂(u,v)=−1.\frac{\partial(P,Q)}{\partial(s,L)}=-2L,\qquad\frac{\partial(s,L)}{\partial(e,L)}=L,\qquad\frac{\partial(e,L)}{\partial(u,v)}=-1.

∎

Remark 7.2.

Thm 7.1 explains the cancellation Eq. 6: it is the condition Jac=κ​Λ2\Jac=\kappa\Lambda^{2} made explicit. It also inverts into a recipe: to build an equivariant Keller map of this weight type, solve the two-dimensional problem Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=κ​Λ2\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=\kappa\Lambda^{2} — a Jacobian problem with prescribed divisorial vanishing along the contracted line — and lift. More generally, it reduces the Jacobian problem for hyperbolically graded maps of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} to a degenerate Jacobian problem on the (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional quotient. We do not know whether the exponent 22 admits a uniform description in terms of the weights; this is the first question the reduction raises.

8. The parameter variety of graded Keller maps

Theorem 7.1 reduces the construction of a graded Keller map to a problem on the invariant quotient. We make that reduction explicit for an arbitrary hyperbolic signature and observe that the resulting condition is trilinear in its unknowns. The graded Keller maps of bounded degree are therefore the points of an explicit multiprojective variety defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and the question of whether Eq. 1 is isolated becomes a question about the rational points of that variety. This is the form in which the two settings of Sec. 11 are most closely comparable: the arithmetic of the hyperbolic example is governed by a parameter space which is itself of the positive-weight type studied in [11].

8.1. Descent for an arbitrary signature

Fix integers r,s>0r,s>0. We have the action of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} on ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} via 𝔾m×ℂ3→ℂ3\mathbb{G}_{m}\times\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} given by

(t,(x1,x2,x3))↦(t​x1,t−r​x2,t−s​x3).(t,(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}))\mapsto\bigl(tx_{1},\;t^{-r}x_{2},\;t^{-s}x_{3}\bigr).

For any t∈𝔾mt\in\mathbb{G}_{m} denote by σt:ℂ3→ℂ3\sigma_{t}:\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} the map given by

σt​(x1,x2,x3)=(t​x1,t−r​x2,t−s​x3).\sigma_{t}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=\bigl(tx_{1},\;t^{-r}x_{2},\;t^{-s}x_{3}\bigr).

On the image ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} we have the action of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} via 𝔾m×ℂ3→ℂ3\mathbb{G}_{m}\times\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} given by

(t,(x1,x2,x3))↦(t−s​x1,t−r​x2,t​x3),(t,(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}))\mapsto\bigl(t^{-s}x_{1},\;t^{-r}x_{2},\;tx_{3}\bigr),

that is the reversal degree type (−s,−r,1)(-s,-r,1) of Lem 2.2. For any t∈𝔾mt\in\mathbb{G}_{m} denote by τt:ℂ3→ℂ3\tau_{t}:\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} the map given by

τt​(x1,x2,x3)=(t−s​x1,t−r​x2,t​x3).\tau_{t}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=\bigl(t^{-s}x_{1},\;t^{-r}x_{2},\;tx_{3}\bigr).

By Cor 2.3 the target weights of a graded Keller map are a permutation of the source weights, and by Lem 2.2 the permutation is determined once the wiw_{i} are distinct. We fix the reversal here because it is the type of Eq. 1, but nothing below depends on that choice. What the descent uses is only that exactly one coordinate on each side carries the positive weight 11, and the computation is unchanged if that coordinate is given a different index. The identity type, in which the positive weight stays in the first position on both sides, occurs in Rem 3.3 and is the setting of Rem 8.4.

Lemma 8.1.

The elements σt,τt\sigma_{t},\tau_{t} are conjugated in Aut⁡(ℂ3)\Aut(\mathbb{C}^{3}) by

w=(001010100)∈GL3⁡(ℂ).w=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\end{pmatrix}\in\GL_{3}(\mathbb{C}).

In other words, τt=w∘σt∘w−1\tau_{t}=w\circ\sigma_{t}\circ w^{-1} for every t∈𝔾mt\in\mathbb{G}_{m}.

Proof.

In the coordinates x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} both actions are diagonal,

σt=diag⁡(t,t−r,t−s),τt=diag⁡(t−s,t−r,t).\sigma_{t}=\diag\bigl(t,\;t^{-r},\;t^{-s}\bigr),\qquad\tau_{t}=\diag\bigl(t^{-s},\;t^{-r},\;t\bigr).

Since w2=idw^{2}=\id we have w−1=ww^{-1}=w, and for any d1,d2,d3d_{1},d_{2},d_{3} one checks directly that

w​diag⁡(d1,d2,d3)​w−1=diag⁡(d3,d2,d1).w\,\diag(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})\,w^{-1}=\diag(d_{3},d_{2},d_{1}).

Applying this with (d1,d2,d3)=(t,t−r,t−s)(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})=(t,t^{-r},t^{-s}) gives w​σt​w−1=τtw\,\sigma_{t}\,w^{-1}=\tau_{t}. ∎

8.1.1. Action on the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]

Grade ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] by the weight defined in Sec. 2, extended to general r,sr,s: the monomial xi​yj​zℓx^{i}y^{j}z^{\ell} has weight i−r​j−s​ℓi-rj-s\ell. The action σ\sigma extends to ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] by σt∗​f=f∘σt\sigma_{t}^{*}f=f\circ\sigma_{t}, which is an action since 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} is commutative, and then σt∗\sigma_{t}^{*} multiplies a monomial by ti−r​j−s​ℓt^{\,i-rj-s\ell}, that is by tt to its weight. We write ℂ​[x,y,z]σ\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]^{\sigma} for the ring of polynomials invariant under σt∗\sigma_{t}^{*} for every tt, that is the polynomials of weight 00. A monomial xi​yj​zℓx^{i}y^{j}z^{\ell} is invariant if and only if i=r​j+s​ℓi=rj+s\ell, so

ℂ​[x,y,z]σ=ℂ⁡[u,v],u=xr​y,v=xs​z,\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]^{\sigma}=\mathbb{C}[u,v],\qquad u=x^{r}y,\quad v=x^{s}z,

freely, for every r,sr,s.

In the same way τ\tau extends to ℂ⁡[a,b,c]\mathbb{C}[a,b,c] by τt∗​f=f∘τt\tau_{t}^{*}f=f\circ\tau_{t}, the monomial ai​bj​cℓa^{i}b^{j}c^{\ell} has weight ℓ−s​i−r​j\ell-si-rj, and we write ℂ​[a,b,c]τ\mathbb{C}[a,b,c]^{\tau} for the ring of polynomials invariant under τt∗\tau_{t}^{*} for every tt. A monomial ai​bj​cℓa^{i}b^{j}c^{\ell} is invariant if and only if ℓ=s​i+r​j\ell=si+rj, so

ℂ​[a,b,c]τ=ℂ⁡[P,Q],P=b​cr,Q=a​cs,\mathbb{C}[a,b,c]^{\tau}=\mathbb{C}[P,Q],\qquad P=b\,c^{\,r},\quad Q=a\,c^{\,s},

freely. For (r,s)=(1,2)(r,s)=(1,2) these are the invariants of Sec. 7.

A polynomial map G=(G1,G2,G3)G=(G_{1},G_{2},G_{3}) is equivariant for (σ,τ)(\sigma,\tau) exactly when each component is weight-homogeneous of the weight of the corresponding image coordinate, that is G1G_{1} of weight −s-s, G2G_{2} of weight −r-r, and G3G_{3} of weight 11: this is the content of the equivariance G∘σt=τt∘GG\circ\sigma_{t}=\tau_{t}\circ G, read one coordinate at a time.

We describe the three graded pieces. A monomial of weight 11 has xx-exponent i=1+r​j+s​ℓ≥1i=1+rj+s\ell\geq 1, so it is xx times an invariant, and the weight-11 piece is x​ℂ​[u,v]x\,\mathbb{C}[u,v]. For the other two, write the monomials of ℂ⁡[u,v]\mathbb{C}[u,v] as ui​vj=xr​i+s​j​yi​zju^{i}v^{j}=x^{ri+sj}y^{i}z^{j}. Then x−r​ui​vjx^{-r}u^{i}v^{j} is a polynomial exactly when r​i+s​j≥rri+sj\geq r, and x−s​ui​vjx^{-s}u^{i}v^{j} exactly when r​i+s​j≥sri+sj\geq s, so the weight-(−r)(-r) piece is x−r​VBx^{-r}V_{B} and the weight-(−s)(-s) piece is x−s​VAx^{-s}V_{A}, where

VB:=span⁡{ui​vj:r​i+s​j≥r},VA:=span⁡{ui​vj:r​i+s​j≥s}.V_{B}:=\Span\bigl\{u^{i}v^{j}:\ ri+sj\geq r\bigr\},\qquad V_{A}:=\Span\bigl\{u^{i}v^{j}:\ ri+sj\geq s\bigr\}.

(9) G=(x−s​A,x−r​B,x​Λ),A∈VA,B∈VB,Λ∈ℂ⁡[u,v],G=\bigl(x^{-s}A,\;x^{-r}B,\;x\Lambda\bigr),\qquad A\in V_{A},\quad B\in V_{B},\quad\Lambda\in\mathbb{C}[u,v],

Proposition 8.2.

For GG as in Eq. 9, up to a universal sign,

detJ​G=±Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)Λr+s−1.\det JG=\pm\,\frac{\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)}{\Lambda^{\,r+s-1}}.

Let A,B,Λ∈ℂ⁡[u,v]A,B,\Lambda\in\mathbb{C}[u,v] and write {f,g}=fu​gv−fv​gu\{f,g\}=f_{u}g_{v}-f_{v}g_{u}. Then

(10) Λ⁡{B,A}+s​A​{B,Λ}+r​B​{Λ,A}=κfor some ​κ∈ℂ×.\Lambda\{B,A\}\;+\;sA\{B,\Lambda\}\;+\;rB\{\Lambda,A\}\;=\;\kappa\qquad\text{for some }\kappa\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}.

{Λr,A​Λs}=Λs​{Λr,A}=r​Λr+s−1​{Λ,A}\{\Lambda^{r},A\Lambda^{s}\}=\Lambda^{s}\{\Lambda^{r},A\}=r\Lambda^{r+s-1}\{\Lambda,A\}

and for Eq. 1 one computes κ=2\kappa=2, recovering Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)=2​L2\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q)=2L^{2} of Thm 7.1.

Remark 8.4.

Proposition 8.2 answers the question raised in Rem 7.2: the exponent is determined by the signature. Let wt⁡(x,y2,…,yn)=(1,−r2,…,−rn)\wt(x,y_{2},\dots,y_{n})=(1,-r_{2},\dots,-r_{n}) with ri>0r_{i}>0, let ui=xri​yiu_{i}=x^{r_{i}}y_{i} be the invariants, and let the target weights be the identity permutation of the source weights, so that the coordinate of weight 11 is again the first. Writing G1=x​ΛG_{1}=x\Lambda and Pi=Gi​G1ri=Bi​ΛriP_{i}=G_{i}G_{1}^{r_{i}}=B_{i}\Lambda^{r_{i}} for i≥2i\geq 2, the same computation gives

The exponent is m−1m-1, which is 22 for the weights wt=(1,−1,−2)\wt=(1,-1,-2); for n=3n=3 one has m=r+sm=r+s, in agreement with Prop 8.2. That the positive weight equals 11 is what makes the quotient again an affine space: already for weights (2,−1,−1)(2,-1,-1) the invariant ring is ℂ⁡[x​y2,x​y​z,x​z2]\mathbb{C}[xy^{2},xyz,xz^{2}], a quadric cone, and the reduction takes place on a singular quotient.

8.2. The base point

The conditions A∈VAA\in V_{A}, B∈VBB\in V_{B} are not merely technical; they pin down a marked point.

Let GG be as in Eq. 9 and suppose Eq. 10 holds. Let O=(0,0)O=(0,0) be the origin of 𝔸u,v2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{u,v}. Then

Thus (A,B)(A,B) is a pair of polynomials with a common zero at which it is étale, and Λ\Lambda does not vanish there. Conversely:

Theorem 8.7.

Let GG be as in Eq. 9, satisfying Eq. 10, with Λ∉ℂ\Lambda\notin\mathbb{C}. Then GG is a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, of degree deg⁡G=deg⁡G¯≥2\deg G=\deg\overline{G}\geq 2.

Proof.

GG is Keller by Thm 8.3, hence dominant, and deg⁡G=deg⁡G¯\deg G=\deg\overline{G} by the argument of Prop 4.3, which uses only Ω=Ωσ​(c)\Omega=\Omega^{\sigma}(c), K=Kτ​(c)K=K^{\tau}(c) and Lem 4.2, and so applies verbatim to any (r,s)(r,s). Suppose deg⁡G=1\deg G=1. Then GG is birational and étale, hence an open immersion by Zariski’s main theorem, and its image UU is isomorphic to ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3}, in particular affine; so ℂ3∖U\mathbb{C}^{3}\setminus U is either empty or a hypersurface V⁡(h)V(h) with hh nonconstant, the complement of an affine open subset of a smooth variety being pure of codimension one. In the latter case hh is a nonconstant unit of 𝒪⁡(U)\mathcal{O}(U), contradicting U≅ℂ3U\cong\mathbb{C}^{3}. Hence U=ℂ3U=\mathbb{C}^{3} and GG is an automorphism.

Its inverse is again equivariant, by the argument in the last step of Thm 3.1, so (G−1)∗(G^{-1})^{*} preserves weights and therefore carries ℂ⁡[u,v]=ℂ​[x,y,z]σ\mathbb{C}[u,v]=\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]^{\sigma} into ℂ​[a,b,c]τ=ℂ⁡[P,Q]\mathbb{C}[a,b,c]^{\tau}=\mathbb{C}[P,Q]; this restriction is inverse to G¯∗\overline{G}^{*}, so G¯\overline{G} is an automorphism of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} and Jacu,v⁡(P,Q)\Jac_{u,v}(P,Q) is a nonzero constant. By Thm 8.3 that constant equals κ​Λr+s−1\kappa\Lambda^{\,r+s-1}, and r+s−1≥1r+s-1\geq 1, so Λ\Lambda is constant, against the hypothesis. Thus deg⁡G≥2\deg G\geq 2 and GG is not injective. ∎

In the graded setting there is therefore no separate injectivity condition to impose: non-injectivity is a consequence of Eq. 10 together with Λ∉ℂ\Lambda\notin\mathbb{C}. The construction of graded counterexamples is the solution of one scalar equation.

Remark 8.8.

The map of Rem 3.3 illustrates the role of Λ\Lambda. There 𝐪=𝐰\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{w}, so the weight-one component is G1G_{1} and the notation is that of Rem 8.4, with (r2,r3,r4,r5)=(1,2,3,4)(r_{2},r_{3},r_{4},r_{5})=(1,2,3,4) and m=∑i≥2ri=10m=\sum_{i\geq 2}r_{i}=10. The invariants are ui=X1ri​Xiu_{i}=X_{1}^{r_{i}}X_{i}, and G1=X1G_{1}=X_{1} gives Λ=1\Lambda=1. Writing Pi=Gi​G1ri=Bi​ΛriP_{i}=G_{i}G_{1}^{r_{i}}=B_{i}\Lambda^{r_{i}} one finds

B2=u2+u3,B3=u3+u4+12​u22,B4=u4+u5−u2​u3,B5=u5+12​u32,B_{2}=u_{2}+u_{3},\quad B_{3}=u_{3}+u_{4}+\tfrac{1}{2}u_{2}^{2},\quad B_{4}=u_{4}+u_{5}-u_{2}u_{3},\quad B_{5}=u_{5}+\tfrac{1}{2}u_{3}^{2},

and a direct computation gives Jacu⁡(B2,…,B5)=1=Λm−1\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,B_{5})=1=\Lambda^{\,m-1}, so detJ​G=1\det JG=1 as it must be. Here Λ\Lambda is constant, so the hypothesis of Thm 8.7 fails, and indeed GG is an automorphism. More generally, when Λ\Lambda is constant Eq. 10 reduces to Jacu⁡(B2,…,Bn)=κ\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,B_{n})=\kappa, which is the Keller condition for G¯\overline{G} alone: the graded problem in dimension nn becomes the ordinary Jacobian Conjecture in dimension n−1n-1, with no contracted locus and no degeneracy. The contracted line of Eq. 1, and not the hyperbolic signature, is what makes a counterexample possible.

8.3. The parameter variety

Fix r,sr,s and a bound 𝐝=(d1,d2,d3)\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}), and set

VA​(𝐝)=VA∩ℂ​[u,v]≤d1,VB​(𝐝)=VB∩ℂ​[u,v]≤d2,VΛ​(𝐝)=ℂ​[u,v]≤d3,V_{A}(\mathbf{d})=V_{A}\cap\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq d_{1}},\quad V_{B}(\mathbf{d})=V_{B}\cap\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq d_{2}},\quad V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})=\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq d_{3}},

μ⁡(A,B,Λ)=Λ⁡{B,A}+s​A​{B,Λ}+r​B​{Λ,A}∈ℂ​[u,v]≤D,\mu(A,B,\Lambda)=\Lambda\{B,A\}+sA\{B,\Lambda\}+rB\{\Lambda,A\}\;\in\;\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq D},

and D=d1+d2+d3−2D=d_{1}+d_{2}+d_{3}-2. Each term of μ\mu is linear in each of AA, BB, Λ\Lambda separately: μ\mu is trilinear. Writing
