each μi​j\mu_{ij} is a form of tridegree (1,1,1)(1,1,1) with coefficients in ℤ⁡[r,s]\mathbb{Z}[r,s]. We define

𝒴r,s,𝐝⊆ℙ⁡(VA​(𝐝))×ℙ⁡(VB​(𝐝))×ℙ⁡(VΛ​(𝐝))\mathcal{Y}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}\;\subseteq\;\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{A}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)\times\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{B}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)\times\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)

to be the closed subscheme cut out by the (D+22)−1\binom{D+2}{2}-1 multihomogeneous equations μi​j=0\mu_{ij}=0, 1≤i+j≤D1\leq i+j\leq D, and 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} to be the open subscheme on which μ00≠0\mu_{00}\neq 0 and deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1. Thus 𝒴r,s,𝐝\mathcal{Y}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} is a multilinear section of a product of projective spaces, defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Theorem 8.9.

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero. There is a bijection between 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘​(k)\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}(k) and the set of Keller maps over kk of the form Eq. 9, graded with source weights 𝐰=(1,−r,−s)\mathbf{w}=(1,-r,-s) and target weights 𝐪=(−s,−r,1)\mathbf{q}=(-s,-r,1), which are not polynomial automorphisms, with deg⁡A≤d1\deg A\leq d_{1}, deg⁡B≤d2\deg B\leq d_{2}, deg⁡Λ≤d3\deg\Lambda\leq d_{3}, taken modulo the scaling action (A,B,Λ)↦(α​A,β​B,γ​Λ)(A,B,\Lambda)\mapsto(\alpha A,\beta B,\gamma\Lambda) of 𝔾m3\mathbb{G}_{m}^{3}.

Proof.

A kk-point of a projective space over a field has kk-rational homogeneous coordinates, so a kk-point of the triple product lifts to a triple (A,B,Λ)(A,B,\Lambda) with coefficients in kk, uniquely up to 𝔾m3​(k)\mathbb{G}_{m}^{3}(k). The conditions μi​j=0\mu_{ij}=0 for (i,j)≠(0,0)(i,j)\neq(0,0) say that μ\mu is the constant κ=μ00\kappa=\mu_{00}, and μ00≠0\mu_{00}\neq 0 says κ∈k×\kappa\in k^{\times}; the triple then defines a Keller map by Thm 8.3, polynomial by the conditions A∈VAA\in V_{A}, B∈VBB\in V_{B}, and graded with the stated weights because Eq. 9 is the description of that graded piece. It is not a polynomial automorphism: the degree degG=[Ω:K]\deg G=[\Omega:K] is unchanged by base change to k¯\bar{k}, so Thm 8.7 applies there and gives deg⁡G≥2\deg G\geq 2, which forbids a polynomial inverse over kk. Conversely such a map determines its triple. Under (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) one has κ↦α​β​γ​κ\kappa\mapsto\alpha\beta\gamma\kappa, so κ\kappa may be normalised to 11 over kk and is not a modulus. ∎

The map FF of Eq. 1 has degu,v⁡A=4\deg_{u,v}A=4, degu,v⁡B=3\deg_{u,v}B=3 and degu,v⁡Λ=1\deg_{u,v}\Lambda=1, so it defines a point

[F]∈𝒴1,2,(4,3,1)∘​(ℚ).[F]\;\in\;\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1)}(\mathbb{Q}).

The function [G]↦degG¯=[ℂ(u,v):ℂ(P,Q)][G]\mapsto\deg\overline{G}=[\mathbb{C}(u,v):\mathbb{C}(P,Q)] is constructible on 𝒴∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ} and stratifies it; by Thm 4.4 the point [F][F] lies in the stratum deg=3\deg=3.

Corollary 8.10.

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero, and fix r,s>0r,s>0 and 𝐝=(d1,d2,d3)\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}). Then there exists a Keller map over kk of the form Eq. 9, graded with source weights 𝐰=(1,−r,−s)\mathbf{w}=(1,-r,-s) and target weights 𝐪=(−s,−r,1)\mathbf{q}=(-s,-r,1), with deg⁡A≤d1\deg A\leq d_{1}, deg⁡B≤d2\deg B\leq d_{2}, deg⁡Λ≤d3\deg\Lambda\leq d_{3}, which is not a polynomial automorphism, if and only if

𝒴r,s,𝐝∘​(k)≠∅.\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}(k)\neq\emptyset.

The Jacobian Conjecture, restricted to graded maps of this weight type and of bounded degree, is therefore the statement that an explicit multiprojective scheme over ℤ\mathbb{Z} has no kk-point.

Remark 8.11.

The two fields behave differently. For k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, or any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the emptiness of 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} is decided by elimination in finitely many steps, so for each fixed (r,s,𝐝)(r,s,\mathbf{d}) the graded Jacobian Conjecture is a finite computation, and the rank criterion of the next subsection is the practical form of it.

For k=ℚk=\mathbb{Q} the same question is a Diophantine problem on a scheme over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and no such procedure is known. This is why we later pass to the weighted height on 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}: it is the right invariant for counting the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-points, and not for deciding whether they exist.

8.4. A determinantal fibration

For fixed BB and Λ\Lambda the expression μ\mu is linear in AA. This gives 𝒴r,s,𝐝\mathcal{Y}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} a fibration by linear spaces over a determinantal base, and turns the search for solutions into linear algebra.

Proposition 8.12.

For (B,Λ)∈VB​(𝐝)×VΛ​(𝐝)(B,\Lambda)\in V_{B}(\mathbf{d})\times V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d}) let

TB,Λ:VA​(𝐝)⟶ℂ​[u,v]≤D,TB,Λ​(A)=μ⁡(A,B,Λ),T_{B,\Lambda}\colon V_{A}(\mathbf{d})\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq D},\qquad T_{B,\Lambda}(A)=\mu(A,B,\Lambda),

a linear map whose matrix entries are bilinear forms in the coefficients of BB and Λ\Lambda, and let

π:ℂ​[u,v]≤D⟶ℂ​[u,v]≤D/ℂ\pi\colon\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq D}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq D}/\mathbb{C}

denote the quotient by the constants. Rescaling BB or Λ\Lambda multiplies TB,ΛT_{B,\Lambda} by a nonzero scalar, so the kernels and ranks below depend only on the classes [B][B] and [Λ][\Lambda]. The projection

𝒴r,s,𝐝⟶ℙ⁡(VB​(𝐝))×ℙ⁡(VΛ​(𝐝))\mathcal{Y}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{B}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)\times\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)

has fibre ℙ⁡(ker⁡(π∘TB,Λ))\mathbb{P}\bigl(\ker(\pi\circ T_{B,\Lambda})\bigr) over ([B],[Λ])([B],[\Lambda]). If moreover deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1, this fibre meets 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} if and only if

rank⁡TB,Λ=rank⁡(π∘TB,Λ)+1.\rank T_{B,\Lambda}=\rank(\pi\circ T_{B,\Lambda})+1.

In particular the locus of ([B],[Λ])([B],[\Lambda]) with deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1 admitting a solution is constructible, defined by the vanishing and the non-vanishing of minors of matrices bilinear in (B,Λ)(B,\Lambda).

Proof.

The fibre is by definition the projectivisation of {A:μ⁡(A,B,Λ)∈ℂ}=ker⁡(π∘TB,Λ)\{A:\mu(A,B,\Lambda)\in\mathbb{C}\}=\ker(\pi\circ T_{B,\Lambda}). Restricted to that kernel, TB,ΛT_{B,\Lambda} takes values in ℂ\mathbb{C}, so its image there is either 00 or all of ℂ\mathbb{C}; the fibre contains a point with κ≠0\kappa\neq 0 exactly in the second case, that is exactly when ker⁡(π∘TB,Λ)⊈ker⁡TB,Λ\ker(\pi\circ T_{B,\Lambda})\not\subseteq\ker T_{B,\Lambda}. By rank–nullity,

dimker⁡(π∘TB,Λ)−dimker⁡TB,Λ=rank⁡TB,Λ−rank⁡(π∘TB,Λ)∈{0,1},\dim\ker(\pi\circ T_{B,\Lambda})-\dim\ker T_{B,\Lambda}=\rank T_{B,\Lambda}-\rank(\pi\circ T_{B,\Lambda})\in\{0,1\},

so that inclusion fails precisely when the difference of ranks equals 11. Since deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1 by hypothesis, κ≠0\kappa\neq 0 is the only remaining condition defining 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}, which gives the stated equivalence. The entries of TB,ΛT_{B,\Lambda} in the monomial bases are the coefficients of μ⁡(ui​vj,B,Λ)\mu(u^{i}v^{j},B,\Lambda), bilinear in (B,Λ)(B,\Lambda) by trilinearity of μ\mu. ∎

The hypothesis deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1 cannot be dropped. If Λ\Lambda is a nonzero constant then {B,Λ}={Λ,A}=0\{B,\Lambda\}=\{\Lambda,A\}=0, so Eq. 10 reduces to

{B,A}=κ/Λ,\{B,A\}=\kappa/\Lambda,

the Keller condition for the pair (A,B)(A,B) on 𝔸u,v2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{u,v} alone, as in Rem 8.8. That stratum is nonempty and contains no counterexample: already A=vA=v, B=uB=u, Λ=1\Lambda=1 satisfies it, with G=(z,y,x)G=(z,y,x) the reversal of the coordinates. Searching it would be searching the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension two.

Proposition 8.12 is the practical form of the recipe of Rem 7.2: to search for graded counterexamples of bounded degree one runs over the coefficients of BB and Λ\Lambda with deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1 and imposes a rank jump, rather than computing a Gröbner basis of the full trilinear system.

8.5. Excess intersection

The system Eq. 10 is heavily overdetermined at the degrees of Eq. 1. For (r,s)=(1,2)(r,s)=(1,2) and 𝐝=(4,3,1)\mathbf{d}=(4,3,1) one has

dimVA​(𝐝)=13,dimVB​(𝐝)=9,dimVΛ​(𝐝)=3,\dim V_{A}(\mathbf{d})=13,\qquad\dim V_{B}(\mathbf{d})=9,\qquad\dim V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})=3,

since ℂ​[u,v]≤4\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq 4} has dimension 1515 and VAV_{A} omits from it only the monomials 11 and uu, while ℂ​[u,v]≤3\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq 3} has dimension 1010 and VBV_{B} omits only 11. The ambient product ℙ12×ℙ8×ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{12}\times\mathbb{P}^{8}\times\mathbb{P}^{2} therefore has dimension 2222, while D=6D=6 and the number of equations is (82)−1=27\binom{8}{2}-1=27. A generic system of 2727 forms of tridegree (1,1,1)(1,1,1) on a 2222-dimensional variety has empty intersection; the expected dimension is −5-5. The existence of Eq. 1 is therefore an excess intersection.

The discrepancy is in fact larger, because 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} is not a bare intersection: the group 𝒢\mathcal{G} described below acts on it, and for 𝐝=(4,3,1)\mathbf{d}=(4,3,1) the subgroup preserving the degree bounds is the linear one, of dimension 33. A nonempty 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} thus contains an entire orbit, and the gap from the expected dimension is at least 55 together with the dimension of that orbit. The sharp form of the question left open in Sec. 11 is the following.

Remark 8.13.

Is 𝒴1,2,(4,3,1)∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1)} a single orbit of the group of liftable automorphisms? More generally, for which signatures (r,s)(r,s) and bounds 𝐝\mathbf{d} is 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} nonempty, and when is it positive-dimensional modulo that group?

The group in question is the one induced on 𝔸u,v2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{u,v} by the graded automorphisms of 𝔸𝐰3\mathbb{A}^{3}_{\mathbf{w}}, that is by the equivariant automorphisms of ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} in the sense of Sec. 2. Such an automorphism has target weights equal to its source weights, so it takes the form x↦x​ϕx\mapsto x\phi, y↦x−r​ψy\mapsto x^{-r}\psi, z↦x−s​χz\mapsto x^{-s}\chi with ϕ,ψ,χ\phi,\psi,\chi invariant. By the argument in the second paragraph of the proof of Thm 8.7, it descends to an automorphism of 𝔸u,v2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{u,v}, whose Jacobian is a nonzero constant; and by Rem 8.4, with n=3n=3 and m=r+sm=r+s,

Jacu,v⁡(ψ​ϕr,χ​ϕs)=κ′​ϕr+s−1.\Jac_{u,v}\bigl(\psi\phi^{r},\,\chi\phi^{s}\bigr)=\kappa^{\prime}\phi^{\,r+s-1}.

The left-hand side is constant and r+s−1≥1r+s-1\geq 1, so ϕ\phi is constant. The induced subgroup of Aut⁡(𝔸2)\Aut(\mathbb{A}^{2}) is therefore contained in

𝒢={φ∈Aut(𝔸2):φ(O)=O,φ∗VA⊆VA,φ∗VB⊆VB},\mathcal{G}=\bigl\{\varphi\in\Aut(\mathbb{A}^{2}):\varphi(O)=O,\ \varphi^{*}V_{A}\subseteq V_{A},\ \varphi^{*}V_{B}\subseteq V_{B}\bigr\},

and in fact equals it: given such a φ\varphi, the monomials uu and vv lie in VBV_{B} and VAV_{A} respectively, so φ1=φ∗​u∈VB\varphi_{1}=\varphi^{*}u\in V_{B} and φ2=φ∗​v∈VA\varphi_{2}=\varphi^{*}v\in V_{A}, and

φ~​(x,y,z)=(x,x−r​φ1​(u,v),x−s​φ2​(u,v))\tilde{\varphi}(x,y,z)=\bigl(x,\;x^{-r}\varphi_{1}(u,v),\;x^{-s}\varphi_{2}(u,v)\bigr)

is a polynomial equivariant map inducing φ\varphi, invertible because φ\varphi is. For (r,s)=(1,2)(r,s)=(1,2) the conditions read φ⁡(O)=O\varphi(O)=O together with φ∗​(u2,v)⊆(u2,v)\varphi^{*}(u^{2},v)\subseteq(u^{2},v), and since φ12\varphi_{1}^{2} lies in (u2,v)(u^{2},v) automatically, they amount to ∂uφ2​(O)=0\partial_{u}\varphi_{2}(O)=0: 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the group of automorphisms fixing OO for which ∂u\partial_{u} is an eigenvector of the differential at OO.

8.6. Weighted heights on the parameter variety

The tori of both actions act on the parameter space, and their quotient is of the positive-weight type of [11].

Let δλ,ρ,ς​(x,y,z)=(λ​x,ρ​y,ς​z)\delta_{\lambda,\rho,\varsigma}(x,y,z)=(\lambda x,\rho y,\varsigma z) and let ϵα,β,γ\epsilon_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma} be the analogous automorphism of the target; both are equivariant, and G↦ϵ∘G∘δ−1G\mapsto\epsilon\circ G\circ\delta^{-1} acts on triples by

Ai​j↦α​λs−r​i−s​j​ρ−i​ς−j​Ai​j,Bi​j↦β​λr−r​i−s​j​ρ−i​ς−j​Bi​j,Λi​j↦γ​λ−1−r​i−s​j​ρ−i​ς−j​Λi​j,\begin{split}A_{ij}&\mapsto\alpha\lambda^{\,s-ri-sj}\rho^{-i}\varsigma^{-j}A_{ij},\\ B_{ij}&\mapsto\beta\lambda^{\,r-ri-sj}\rho^{-i}\varsigma^{-j}B_{ij},\\ \Lambda_{ij}&\mapsto\gamma\lambda^{-1-ri-sj}\rho^{-i}\varsigma^{-j}\Lambda_{ij},\end{split}

the subscripts indexing the coefficient of ui​vju^{i}v^{j}. The one-parameter subgroup λ=1\lambda=1, ρ=ς=t−1\rho=\varsigma=t^{-1}, α=β=γ=t\alpha=\beta=\gamma=t acts on every coefficient by t 1+i+jt^{\,1+i+j}.

Proposition 8.14.

Let

N=dimVA​(𝐝)+dimVB​(𝐝)+dimVΛ​(𝐝)N=\dim V_{A}(\mathbf{d})+\dim V_{B}(\mathbf{d})+\dim V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})

and let 𝛚∈ℤ>0N\boldsymbol{\omega}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{N} be the vector whose entry at the coordinate indexing the coefficient of ui​vju^{i}v^{j} equals 1+i+j1+i+j. Then the 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action above identifies

(VA​(𝐝)⊕VB​(𝐝)⊕VΛ​(𝐝))∖{0}/𝔾m=𝕎​ℙ​(𝝎),\bigl(V_{A}(\mathbf{d})\oplus V_{B}(\mathbf{d})\oplus V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)\setminus\{0\}\;\big/\;\mathbb{G}_{m}\;=\;\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}),

a weighted projective space, well-formed when d1≥2d_{1}\geq 2 and d3≥1d_{3}\geq 1, and the equation μi​j=0\mu_{ij}=0 is homogeneous for it of weighted degree 5+i+j5+i+j. The graded Keller counterexamples of bounded degree are therefore parametrised by a locally closed subvariety 𝒲r,s,𝐝⊆𝕎​ℙ​(𝛚)\mathcal{W}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}\subseteq\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

All the exponents 1+i+j1+i+j are positive, so the quotient of the punctured affine space by the displayed 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action is by definition the weighted projective space 𝕎​ℙ​(𝝎)\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}). The coefficient Λ00\Lambda_{00} occurs, since VΛ​(𝐝)=ℂ​[u,v]≤d3V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})=\mathbb{C}[u,v]_{\leq d_{3}} contains the constants, and carries weight 11; hence the action is faithful and no reduction of the weights is needed. For well-formedness one must check that any N−1N-1 of the weights have greatest common divisor 11. A subset containing the coordinate Λ00\Lambda_{00} has gcd=1\gcd=1 at once. Its complement contains Λ10\Lambda_{10}, of weight 22, when d3≥1d_{3}\geq 1, and v2∈VA​(𝐝)v^{2}\in V_{A}(\mathbf{d}), of weight 33, when d1≥2d_{1}\geq 2; these are coprime.

For the homogeneity, write A=∑Ai​j​ui​vjA=\sum A_{ij}u^{i}v^{j}. Under the subgroup,

A′​(u,v)=∑t 1+i+j​Ai​j​ui​vj=t​A​(t​u,t​v),A^{\prime}(u,v)=\sum t^{\,1+i+j}A_{ij}u^{i}v^{j}=t\,A(tu,tv),

and likewise B′​(u,v)=t​B​(t​u,t​v)B^{\prime}(u,v)=t\,B(tu,tv) and Λ′​(u,v)=t​Λ​(t​u,t​v)\Lambda^{\prime}(u,v)=t\,\Lambda(tu,tv). Differentiating, ∂uA′=t2​Au​(t​u,t​v)\partial_{u}A^{\prime}=t^{2}A_{u}(tu,tv) and similarly for the other first derivatives, so each bracket satisfies {B′,A′}=t4​{B,A}​(t​u,t​v)\{B^{\prime},A^{\prime}\}=t^{4}\{B,A\}(tu,tv). Each of the three terms of μ\mu is a bracket multiplied by one of A,B,ΛA,B,\Lambda, so

μ⁡(A′,B′,Λ′)​(u,v)=t5​μ​(A,B,Λ)​(t​u,t​v),\mu(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},\Lambda^{\prime})(u,v)=t^{5}\,\mu(A,B,\Lambda)(tu,tv),

and comparing coefficients of ui​vju^{i}v^{j} gives μi​j↦t 5+i+j​μi​j\mu_{ij}\mapsto t^{\,5+i+j}\mu_{ij}. The locus 𝒲r,s,𝐝\mathcal{W}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} is then cut out by these homogeneous equations together with the open conditions μ00≠0\mu_{00}\neq 0 and deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1, all defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}. ∎

The quotient here is not the one of Thm 8.9. Both are quotients of the affine cone of triples satisfying Eq. 10, but 𝒴r,s,𝐝\mathcal{Y}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} divides by the group 𝔾m3\mathbb{G}_{m}^{3} rescaling AA, BB and Λ\Lambda separately, whereas 𝕎​ℙ​(𝝎)\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) divides by the single 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} above, which acts on the coefficient of ui​vju^{i}v^{j} by t 1+i+jt^{\,1+i+j} and is therefore not a subgroup of 𝔾m3\mathbb{G}_{m}^{3}. For 𝐝=(4,3,1)\mathbf{d}=(4,3,1) the two ambient spaces have dimensions 2222 and 2424. A point of 𝒲r,s,𝐝\mathcal{W}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} is thus a triple taken modulo less than a point of 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}, and the counting function below counts these finer objects; passing to genuine equivalence classes of maps would require dividing further, by the remaining torus and by 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

The weighted height of [2, 11] is nevertheless the natural height on 𝕎​ℙ​(𝝎)\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}), and one may ask for the asymptotics of

𝒩⁡(X)=#⁡{[G]∈𝒲r,s,𝐝​(ℚ):𝔥𝐰​([G])≤X}.\mathcal{N}(X)=\#\bigl\{[G]\in\mathcal{W}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}(\mathbb{Q}):\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbf{w}}([G])\leq X\bigr\}.

Unlike the counting function Z⁡(X)Z(X) of Sec. 11, this one is well posed: 𝕎​ℙ​(𝝎)\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) is proper and the weights 𝝎\boldsymbol{\omega} are positive, so no height theory for hyperbolic quotients is required. The hyperbolic example is counted by an elliptic parameter space. If Rem 8.13 has the answer that 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} is a single 𝒢\mathcal{G}-orbit, then 𝒩⁡(X)\mathcal{N}(X) measures the growth of that orbit together with the fibres of 𝒲r,s,𝐝→𝒴∘\mathcal{W}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}\to\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}, and nothing more; if not, its exponent should again come from a linear program, as in the positive-weight setting.

8.7. Field of moduli

Since 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} are defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, the quotient carries a field of moduli for each graded counterexample, and one may ask whether it is a field of definition. It is convenient to work with the group upstairs. Let 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp} denote the group of pairs (δ,ϵ)(\delta,\epsilon) of equivariant polynomial automorphisms of the source and the target ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3}, acting on maps by G↦ϵ∘G∘δ−1G\mapsto\epsilon\circ G\circ\delta^{-1}, and let Aut♯⁡(G)\Aut^{\sharp}(G) be the stabiliser of GG. Write Γ=Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\Gamma=\Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}). The obstruction to descending GG from a field of definition to its field of moduli lies in H1​(Γ,Aut♯⁡(G))H^{1}\bigl(\Gamma,\Aut^{\sharp}(G)\bigr).

Here the grading intervenes. By Eq. 4 the pair (σt,τt)(\sigma_{t},\tau_{t}) satisfies τt∘G∘σt−1=G\tau_{t}\circ G\circ\sigma_{t}^{-1}=G for every tt, so t↦(σt,τt)t\mapsto(\sigma_{t},\tau_{t}) embeds 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} in Aut♯⁡(G)\Aut^{\sharp}(G), for every graded GG at once. This 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} acts trivially on 𝔸u,v2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{u,v}, since uu and vv are invariants; it is the kernel of the homomorphism 𝒢♯→𝒢\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}\to\mathcal{G} of Sec. 8, and by the computation there, which forces ϕ\phi to be constant, that homomorphism is surjective with 𝒢=𝒢♯/𝔾m\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}^{\sharp}/\mathbb{G}_{m}. From the exact sequence

1⟶𝔾m⟶Aut♯⁡(G)⟶π0⟶1,1\longrightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}\longrightarrow\Aut^{\sharp}(G)\longrightarrow\pi_{0}\longrightarrow 1,

where π0\pi_{0} is the image of Aut♯⁡(G)\Aut^{\sharp}(G) in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, one obtains the exact sequence of pointed sets

H1​(Γ,𝔾m)⟶H1​(Γ,Aut♯⁡(G))⟶H1​(Γ,π0),H^{1}(\Gamma,\mathbb{G}_{m})\longrightarrow H^{1}\bigl(\Gamma,\Aut^{\sharp}(G)\bigr)\longrightarrow H^{1}(\Gamma,\pi_{0}),

and H1​(Γ,𝔾m)=1H^{1}(\Gamma,\mathbb{G}_{m})=1 by Hilbert 90. Exactness at the middle term says that the fibre over the neutral class is trivial; hence a nontrivial obstruction class must have nontrivial image in H1​(Γ,π0)H^{1}(\Gamma,\pi_{0}). The connected part contributes nothing, and any obstruction is detected by the component group.

Remark 8.15.

Compute Aut♯⁡(F)\Aut^{\sharp}(F) for the map Eq. 1. Is it connected, that is, is π0\pi_{0} trivial? If not, the field of moduli of a graded counterexample need not be a field of definition, and the obstruction is a Kummer class of the same kind as the one appearing on the stacky stratum in Rem 5.3, now at the level of moduli rather than of fibres. One may also ask whether every point of 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘​(ℂ)\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}(\mathbb{C}) is defined over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}; this holds whenever 𝒴∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ} is a single 𝒢\mathcal{G}-orbit of a ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-point, and would say that a graded counterexample can carry no transcendental modulus.

9. Higher dimensions

The construction of Sec. 8 is not special to dimension three. We record here that it generalises to ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} for every n≥3n\geq 3, provided the weight vector has exactly one positive entry and that entry equals 11. The master equation stays multilinear, and the parameter variety becomes a multilinear section of a product of nn projective spaces. We also record where the generalisation stops, which sharpens the trichotomy of Sec. 11.

Fix n≥3n\geq 3 and a tuple 𝐫=(r2,…,rn)\mathbf{r}=(r_{2},\dots,r_{n}) of positive integers. Write 𝐰=(1,−r2,…,−rn)\mathbf{w}=(1,-r_{2},\dots,-r_{n}), use x,y2,…,ynx,y_{2},\dots,y_{n} for the coordinates on the source, and set

m=∑i=2nri.m=\sum_{i=2}^{n}r_{i}.

By Cor 2.3 the target weights of a graded Keller map are a permutation of 𝐰\mathbf{w}; relabelling the target coordinates, a graded isomorphism by Cor 2.3(ii), we take 𝐪=𝐰\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{w} and write a1,…,ana_{1},\dots,a_{n} for the target coordinates. For n=3n=3 this is the identity type of Rem 8.4 rather than the reversal of Sec. 8, a difference of labelling only.

For a multi-index 𝐛=(b2,…,bn)\mathbf{b}=(b_{2},\dots,b_{n}) we write u𝐛=u2b2⋯unbnu^{\mathbf{b}}=u_{2}^{b_{2}}\cdots u_{n}^{b_{n}} and |𝐛|=∑ibi|\mathbf{b}|=\sum_{i}b_{i}.

9.1. The graded pieces

A monomial xcy2b2⋯ynbnx^{c}y_{2}^{b_{2}}\cdots y_{n}^{b_{n}} has weight c−∑iri​bic-\sum_{i}r_{i}b_{i}, so it is invariant exactly when c=∑iri​bic=\sum_{i}r_{i}b_{i}, and then it equals u𝐛u^{\mathbf{b}} for

ui=xri​yi.u_{i}=x^{r_{i}}y_{i}.

Hence ℂ​[x,y]σ=ℂ⁡[u2,…,un]\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{\sigma}=\mathbb{C}[u_{2},\dots,u_{n}], freely. The same count gives the pieces we need. A monomial of weight 11 has c=1+∑iri​bi≥1c=1+\sum_{i}r_{i}b_{i}\geq 1, so it is xx times an invariant, and the weight-11 piece is x​ℂ​[u]x\,\mathbb{C}[u]. A monomial of weight −rj-r_{j} has c=∑iri​bi−rjc=\sum_{i}r_{i}b_{i}-r_{j}, which is nonnegative exactly when ∑iri​bi≥rj\sum_{i}r_{i}b_{i}\geq r_{j}, so the weight-(−rj)(-r_{j}) piece is x−rj​Vjx^{-r_{j}}V_{j} with

Vj:=span⁡{u𝐛:∑iri​bi≥rj},V_{j}:=\Span\Bigl\{\,u^{\mathbf{b}}\ :\ \sum_{i}r_{i}b_{i}\geq r_{j}\,\Bigr\},

a monomial ideal of ℂ⁡[u]\mathbb{C}[u]. For n=3n=3, with (r2,r3)=(r,s)(r_{2},r_{3})=(r,s), these are V2=VBV_{2}=V_{B} and V3=VAV_{3}=V_{A}.

A graded polynomial map G:ℂn→ℂnG\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} of this weight type is therefore exactly a tuple

(11) G=(x​Λ,x−r2​B2,…,x−rn​Bn),Λ∈ℂ⁡[u],Bj∈Vj.G=\bigl(x\Lambda,\;x^{-r_{2}}B_{2},\;\dots,\;x^{-r_{n}}B_{n}\bigr),\qquad\Lambda\in\mathbb{C}[u],\quad B_{j}\in V_{j}.

On the target, ℂ​[a]τ=ℂ⁡[P2,…,Pn]\mathbb{C}[a]^{\tau}=\mathbb{C}[P_{2},\dots,P_{n}] freely, with Pj=a1rj​ajP_{j}=a_{1}^{r_{j}}a_{j}, and G∗​Pj=Bj​ΛrjG^{*}P_{j}=B_{j}\Lambda^{r_{j}}; so GG descends to

G¯=(B2​Λr2,…,Bn​Λrn):𝔸un−1⟶𝔸Pn−1.\overline{G}=\bigl(B_{2}\Lambda^{r_{2}},\dots,B_{n}\Lambda^{r_{n}}\bigr)\colon\mathbb{A}^{n-1}_{u}\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n-1}_{P}.

9.2. The master equation

Proposition 9.1.

For GG as in Eq. 11, up to a universal sign,

detJ​G=±Jacu⁡(P2,…,Pn)Λm−1.\det JG=\pm\,\frac{\Jac_{u}(P_{2},\dots,P_{n})}{\Lambda^{\,m-1}}.
Proof.

On {x≠0}\{x\neq 0\} use coordinates (x,u2,…,un)(x,u_{2},\dots,u_{n}). The change (x,y)↦(x,u)(x,y)\mapsto(x,u) has triangular Jacobian matrix with diagonal (1,xr2,…,xrn)(1,x^{r_{2}},\dots,x^{r_{n}}), hence determinant ±xm\pm x^{m}; likewise (a1,…,an)↦(a1,P2,…,Pn)(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\mapsto(a_{1},P_{2},\dots,P_{n}) has determinant ±a1m\pm a_{1}^{m}. In these coordinates GG is

(x,u)⟼(x​Λ​(u),P2​(u),…,Pn​(u)),(x,u)\longmapsto\bigl(x\Lambda(u),\,P_{2}(u),\dots,P_{n}(u)\bigr),

whose Jacobian matrix is block triangular with determinant Λ​Jacu​(P2,…,Pn)\Lambda\Jac_{u}(P_{2},\dots,P_{n}). Since a1=x​Λa_{1}=x\Lambda along GG, the chain rule gives

ΛJacu(P2,…,Pn)=±(xΛ)mdetJGx−m=±ΛmdetJG\Lambda\,\Jac_{u}(P_{2},\dots,P_{n})=\pm\,(x\Lambda)^{m}\,\det JG\,x^{-m}=\pm\,\Lambda^{m}\,\det JG

on a dense open set, hence everywhere, and the claim follows. ∎

This proves the formula asserted in Rem 8.4. The next result is the general form of Thm 8.3.

Theorem 9.2.

Let Λ,B2,…,Bn∈ℂ⁡[u2,…,un]\Lambda,B_{2},\dots,B_{n}\in\mathbb{C}[u_{2},\dots,u_{n}] and set

μ⁡(B2,…,Bn,Λ)=Λ​Jacu​(B2,…,Bn)+∑i=2nri​Bi​Jacu​(B2,…,Λ,…,Bn),\mu(B_{2},\dots,B_{n},\Lambda)=\Lambda\,\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,B_{n})+\sum_{i=2}^{n}r_{i}B_{i}\,\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,\Lambda,\dots,B_{n}),

the ii-th summand having Λ\Lambda in the ii-th slot. Then

Jacu⁡(B2​Λr2,…,Bn​Λrn)=Λm−1​μ​(B2,…,Bn,Λ),\Jac_{u}\bigl(B_{2}\Lambda^{r_{2}},\dots,B_{n}\Lambda^{r_{n}}\bigr)=\Lambda^{\,m-1}\,\mu(B_{2},\dots,B_{n},\Lambda),

and consequently GG as in Eq. 11 is a Keller map if and only if

(12) μ⁡(B2,…,Bn,Λ)=κfor some ​κ∈ℂ×.\mu(B_{2},\dots,B_{n},\Lambda)=\kappa\qquad\text{for some }\kappa\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}.

Moreover μ\mu is multilinear, of multidegree (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\dots,1) in its nn arguments B2,…,Bn,ΛB_{2},\dots,B_{n},\Lambda.

Proof.

Differentiating Pi=Bi​ΛriP_{i}=B_{i}\Lambda^{r_{i}} gives

∂Pi∂uj=Λri−1​(Λ​∂Bi∂uj+ri​Bi​∂Λ∂uj),\frac{\partial P_{i}}{\partial u_{j}}=\Lambda^{\,r_{i}-1}\Bigl(\Lambda\frac{\partial B_{i}}{\partial u_{j}}+r_{i}B_{i}\frac{\partial\Lambda}{\partial u_{j}}\Bigr),

so the ii-th row of the matrix Ju​(P)J_{u}(P) is Λri−1(Λ∇Bi+riBi∇Λ)\Lambda^{\,r_{i}-1}\bigl(\Lambda\nabla B_{i}+r_{i}B_{i}\nabla\Lambda\bigr). Factoring Λri−1\Lambda^{\,r_{i}-1} out of each of the n−1n-1 rows contributes Λm−(n−1)\Lambda^{\,m-(n-1)}. Expanding the remaining determinant by multilinearity in the rows gives 2n−12^{\,n-1} terms, one for each choice of Λ∇Bi\Lambda\nabla B_{i} or riBi∇Λr_{i}B_{i}\nabla\Lambda in each row. Any term choosing riBi∇Λr_{i}B_{i}\nabla\Lambda in two or more rows has two proportional rows and vanishes. The term choosing Λ∇Bi\Lambda\nabla B_{i} in every row is Λn−1​Jacu​(B2,…,Bn)\Lambda^{\,n-1}\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,B_{n}), and the term choosing riBi∇Λr_{i}B_{i}\nabla\Lambda in the single row ii is Λn−2​ri​Bi​Jacu​(B2,…,Λ,…,Bn)\Lambda^{\,n-2}r_{i}B_{i}\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,\Lambda,\dots,B_{n}). Hence

Jacu⁡(P)=Λm−(n−1)⋅Λn−2​μ=Λm−1​μ,\Jac_{u}(P)=\Lambda^{\,m-(n-1)}\cdot\Lambda^{\,n-2}\,\mu=\Lambda^{\,m-1}\,\mu,

and Eq. 12 follows from Prop 9.1. For the multidegree, the first summand is linear in Λ\Lambda and, a determinant being multilinear in its rows, in each BiB_{i}. In the ii-th summand, BiB_{i} occurs once as the outer factor and not inside the determinant, Λ\Lambda occurs once inside it, and each BjB_{j} with j≠ij\neq i occurs once as a row. ∎

For n=3n=3, writing B2=BB_{2}=B, B3=AB_{3}=A and (r2,r3)=(r,s)(r_{2},r_{3})=(r,s), one has Jacu⁡(B2,B3)={B,A}\Jac_{u}(B_{2},B_{3})=\{B,A\} and Eq. 12 reads

Λ⁡{B,A}+r​B​{Λ,A}+s​A​{B,Λ}=κ,\Lambda\{B,A\}+rB\{\Lambda,A\}+sA\{B,\Lambda\}=\kappa,

which is Eq. 10. The map of Rem 3.3 is the case n=5n=5, 𝐫=(1,2,3,4)\mathbf{r}=(1,2,3,4), Λ=1\Lambda=1, computed in Rem 8.8.

9.3. Consequences

Lemma 9.3.

Let GG be as in Eq. 11 and suppose Eq. 12 holds. Let OO be the origin of 𝔸un−1\mathbb{A}^{n-1}_{u}. Then Bi​(O)=0B_{i}(O)=0 for every ii, Λ⁡(O)≠0\Lambda(O)\neq 0, and d​B2∧⋯∧d​Bn|O≠0dB_{2}\wedge\dots\wedge dB_{n}|_{O}\neq 0.

Proof.

Every monomial u𝐛u^{\mathbf{b}} spanning ViV_{i} satisfies ∑jrj​bj≥ri>0\sum_{j}r_{j}b_{j}\geq r_{i}>0, so |𝐛|≥1|\mathbf{b}|\geq 1; hence ViV_{i} contains no constant and lies in (u2,…,un)(u_{2},\dots,u_{n}), giving Bi​(O)=0B_{i}(O)=0. Evaluating Eq. 12 at OO kills every summand of the sum, leaving

Λ⁡(O)​Jacu​(B2,…,Bn)​(O)=κ≠0.\Lambda(O)\,\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,B_{n})(O)=\kappa\neq 0.

∎

Theorem 9.4.

Let GG be as in Eq. 11, satisfying Eq. 12, with Λ∉ℂ\Lambda\notin\mathbb{C}. Then GG is a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture.

Proof.

The argument of Thm 8.7 applies verbatim, Zariski’s main theorem and the unit argument holding in every dimension: were GG injective it would be a polynomial automorphism, its inverse would again be graded, and G¯\overline{G} would be an automorphism of 𝔸n−1\mathbb{A}^{n-1}, so Jacu⁡(P)\Jac_{u}(P) would be a nonzero constant. By Thm 9.2 that constant is κ​Λm−1\kappa\Lambda^{\,m-1}, and m≥n−1≥2m\geq n-1\geq 2, so Λ\Lambda would be constant. ∎

The hypothesis n≥3n\geq 3 enters only through m≥2m\geq 2. For n=2n=2 and r2=1r_{2}=1 the exponent m−1m-1 vanishes and the argument gives nothing, consistently with Thm 3.4, where the hyperbolic case in dimension two admits no counterexample.

Finally, fix a bound 𝐝=(d2,…,dn,dΛ)\mathbf{d}=(d_{2},\dots,d_{n},d_{\Lambda}) and set

Vi​(𝐝)=Vi∩ℂ​[u]≤di,VΛ​(𝐝)=ℂ​[u]≤dΛ,D=dΛ+∑i≥2di−(n−1).V_{i}(\mathbf{d})=V_{i}\cap\mathbb{C}[u]_{\leq d_{i}},\qquad V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})=\mathbb{C}[u]_{\leq d_{\Lambda}},\qquad D=d_{\Lambda}+\sum_{i\geq 2}d_{i}-(n-1).

Writing μ=∑𝐛μ𝐛​u𝐛\mu=\sum_{\mathbf{b}}\mu_{\mathbf{b}}\,u^{\mathbf{b}}, each μ𝐛\mu_{\mathbf{b}} is a form of multidegree (1,…,1)(1,\dots,1) with coefficients in ℤ⁡[r2,…,rn]\mathbb{Z}[r_{2},\dots,r_{n}], by Thm 9.2. The graded Keller counterexamples of this weight type and bounded degree are therefore the points of the open subscheme

𝒴𝐫,𝐝∘⊆ℙ⁡(V2​(𝐝))×⋯×ℙ⁡(Vn​(𝐝))×ℙ⁡(VΛ​(𝐝))\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}}\;\subseteq\;\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{2}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)\times\dots\times\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{n}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)\times\mathbb{P}\bigl(V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})\bigr)

on which μ𝟎≠0\mu_{\mathbf{0}}\neq 0 and deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1, cut out in the ambient product by the (D+n−1n−1)−1\binom{D+n-1}{n-1}-1 equations μ𝐛=0\mu_{\mathbf{b}}=0 with 1≤|𝐛|≤D1\leq|\mathbf{b}|\leq D, and defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}. The proofs of Thm 8.9, Prop 8.12 and Prop 8.14 use only the multilinearity of μ\mu and go through unchanged: fixing all arguments but one leaves a linear map whose rank jump detects κ≠0\kappa\neq 0, and the one-parameter subgroup acting on the coefficient of u𝐛u^{\mathbf{b}} by t 1+|𝐛|t^{\,1+|\mathbf{b}|} presents the whole space as a weighted projective space 𝕎​ℙ​(𝝎)\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) with positive weights 1+|𝐛|1+|\mathbf{b}|, well-formed under a condition on 𝐝\mathbf{d} checked as in Prop 8.14. The computation there generalises to

μ𝐛⟼t 2​n−1+|𝐛|​μ𝐛,\mu_{\mathbf{b}}\longmapsto t^{\,2n-1+|\mathbf{b}|}\mu_{\mathbf{b}},

which is the weighted degree 5+|𝐛|5+|\mathbf{b}| of Prop 8.14 when n=3n=3. For n=3n=3 all of this recovers Sec. 8.

9.4. Where the construction stops

Two hypotheses are doing work, and neither can be dropped by the methods above.

The positive weight must equal 11. It is this that makes the invariants ui=xri​yiu_{i}=x^{r_{i}}y_{i} generate ℂ​[x,y]σ\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{\sigma} freely, so that the quotient is again an affine space and Jacu\Jac_{u} has its usual meaning. Already for 𝐰=(2,−1,−1)\mathbf{w}=(2,-1,-1) the invariant ring is ℂ⁡[x​y2,x​y​z,x​z2]\mathbb{C}[xy^{2},xyz,xz^{2}], a quadric cone, as noted in Rem 8.4; the graded pieces are then modules over a non-polynomial ring rather than monomial ideals, and the passage from Eq. 11 to a linear-algebra problem fails at the first step.

There must be exactly one positive weight. This is what makes the weight-11 piece equal to x​ℂ​[u]x\,\mathbb{C}[u], which produces the factor Λ\Lambda and with it the contracted locus {Λ=0}\{\Lambda=0\}, the object around which all of Sec. 8 is organised. With two positive weights, say 𝐰=(1,1,−1)\mathbf{w}=(1,1,-1), the invariant ring ℂ⁡[x​z,y​z]\mathbb{C}[xz,yz] is still free, so singularity of the quotient is not the obstruction; but the weight-11 piece contains both xx and yy, and yy is not xx times a polynomial invariant. We do not know what replaces Eq. 11 in that case.

Within the hyperbolic case the reduction is therefore governed by more than the signature: by the number of positive weights, and by the value of the positive one. A parameter variety for the remaining hyperbolic signatures would require different methods.

10. Classification of graded Keller maps 𝔸𝐰n→𝔸𝐪n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}}

We now ask the question the previous sections have been preparing: for which data does a graded Keller counterexample exist? The data is a dimension, a weight vector, and a bound on the degrees, and the answer is organised as a descent through that data. At each stage we say what is settled and what is not; Table 1 collects the outcome.

10.1. The classification datum

Let G:𝔸𝐰n→𝔸𝐪nG\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{q}} be a graded Keller map. By Cor 2.3 the vector 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a permutation of 𝐰\mathbf{w}, say 𝐪=π⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{q}=\pi(\mathbf{w}). The permutation is not part of the datum. Indeed, by Cor 2.3(ii) the coordinate permutation π\pi is a graded isomorphism 𝔸π⁡(𝐰)n→𝔸𝐰n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\pi(\mathbf{w})}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}, and composing GG with it changes neither the Keller property nor the property of being a polynomial automorphism; so the families attached to two permutations are identified. We may therefore always normalise 𝐪=𝐰\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{w}, as we did in Eq. 13 below, and the reversal convention of Sec. 8 and the identity convention of Sec. 9 differ only by this identification.

Three further reductions apply. We assume 𝐰≠0\mathbf{w}\neq 0, the case 𝐰=0\mathbf{w}=0 imposing no condition at all and being the Jacobian Conjecture itself in dimension nn. By Cor 2.3(iv) we may normalise gcd⁡(w1,…,wn)=1\gcd(w_{1},\dots,w_{n})=1. Replacing tt by t−1t^{-1} replaces 𝐰\mathbf{w} by −𝐰-\mathbf{w} and changes neither GG nor its being graded, so we may fix the sign of any one nonzero weight. Finally, a permutation of the source coordinates carries 𝔸𝐰n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}} to 𝔸𝐰′n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}} for the correspondingly permuted 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime}, so only the multiset of weights matters.

Write

𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w})

for the set of graded Keller maps 𝔸𝐰n→𝔸𝐰n\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbf{w}} which are not polynomial automorphisms, taken up to the equivalence generated by the graded automorphisms of source and target; that is, up to the group 𝒢♯\mathcal{G}^{\sharp} of Sec. 8, whose image in Aut⁡(𝔸n−1)\Aut(\mathbb{A}^{n-1}) is the group 𝒢\mathcal{G} used in the parameter space. The classification problem is to decide when 𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w}) is empty, and to describe it when it is not.

10.2. First cut: signature and dimension

Theorem 10.1.

Let 𝐰∈ℤn∖{0}\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\setminus\{0\} be a weight vector, normalised as above.

  1. (1)

    If 𝐰\mathbf{w} is elliptic, then 𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)=∅\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w})=\emptyset, for every nn.

  2. (2)

    If n≤2n\leq 2, then 𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)=∅\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w})=\emptyset, for every signature.

Proof.

(1) is Thm 3.1. For (2) with n=2n=2 this is Thm 3.4. For n=1n=1 the normalisation gives 𝐰=(±1)\mathbf{w}=(\pm 1); a Keller map 𝔸1→𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{A}^{1} has constant nonzero derivative, hence is affine, and gradedness with w1≠0w_{1}\neq 0 forces G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0 by Lem 2.1(ii), so GG is linear and invertible. ∎

What remains is n≥3n\geq 3 with 𝐰\mathbf{w} parabolic or hyperbolic.

10.3. Second cut: the parabolic case

Let 𝐰\mathbf{w} be parabolic, let Z={i:wi=0}Z=\{i:w_{i}=0\} and z=#​Z≥1z=\#Z\geq 1, and let 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime} denote the nonzero part, of length n−z≥1n-z\geq 1. Since 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a permutation of 𝐰\mathbf{w}, the target has zz zero weights as well. Two cases occur, according to the signature of 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime}, and both reduce to problems already named.

Theorem 10.2.

Suppose the nonzero weights of 𝐰\mathbf{w} are all of the same sign. Then 𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)≠∅\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w})\neq\emptyset if and only if the Jacobian Conjecture fails in dimension zz. In particular 𝒦⁡(n,𝐰)=∅\mathcal{K}(n,\mathbf{w})=\emptyset when z=1z=1.

Proof.

Replacing tt by t−1t^{-1} we may take the nonzero weights positive. Write the source coordinates as (x,ζ)(x,\zeta), with x=(x1,…,xk)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}) carrying the positive weights, k=n−zk=n-z, and ζ=(ζ1,…,ζz)\zeta=(\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{z}) the weight-zero ones, and the target coordinates likewise. A component of weight 00 is an invariant, hence lies in ℂ⁡[ζ]\mathbb{C}[\zeta]; a component of positive weight has every monomial divisible by some xix_{i}. So

G⁡(x,ζ)=(F⁡(x,ζ),h⁡(ζ)),G(x,\zeta)=\bigl(F(x,\zeta),\,h(\zeta)\bigr),

and J​GJG is block triangular with detJ​G=det(∂F/∂x)⋅det(∂h/∂ζ)\det JG=\det(\partial F/\partial x)\cdot\det(\partial h/\partial\zeta). A product of two polynomials equal to a nonzero constant has both factors nonzero constants, so hh is a Keller map in zz variables and, for each fixed ζ0\zeta_{0}, the map F⁡(⋅,ζ0):𝔸k→𝔸kF(\cdot,\zeta_{0})\colon\mathbb{A}^{k}\to\mathbb{A}^{k} is a Keller map, graded with elliptic weights 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime}. By Thm 3.1 it is an automorphism of 𝔸k\mathbb{A}^{k}.

Hence GG is injective if and only if hh is: one direction is immediate, and if h⁡(ζ)=h⁡(ζ′)h(\zeta)=h(\zeta^{\prime}) with ζ≠ζ′\zeta\neq\zeta^{\prime} then, F⁡(⋅,ζ′)F(\cdot,\zeta^{\prime}) being surjective, any xx admits an x′x^{\prime} with F⁡(x,ζ)=F⁡(x′,ζ′)F(x,\zeta)=F(x^{\prime},\zeta^{\prime}). An injective polynomial self-map of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} is an automorphism [9], so GG is an automorphism exactly when hh is. Conversely, a Keller map hh of 𝔸z\mathbb{A}^{z} which is not an automorphism yields G=(x,h⁡(ζ))G=(x,h(\zeta)), graded for 𝐰=(1,…,1,0,…,0)\mathbf{w}=(1,\dots,1,0,\dots,0) and not an automorphism. For z=1z=1 a Keller map of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} is affine. ∎

Suppose instead that 𝐰′\mathbf{w}^{\prime} is hyperbolic. If 𝐰\mathbf{w} has exactly one positive weight and that weight is 11, so that

𝐰=(1,−r2,…,−rn),ri≥0,\mathbf{w}=(1,-r_{2},\dots,-r_{n}),\qquad r_{i}\geq 0,

then the whole of Sec. 9 applies with ri≥0r_{i}\geq 0 in place of ri>0r_{i}>0. The invariants ui=xri​yiu_{i}=x^{r_{i}}y_{i} still generate ℂ​[x,y]σ\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{\sigma} freely, the weight-11 piece is still x​ℂ​[u]x\,\mathbb{C}[u], and Vi=ℂ⁡[u]V_{i}=\mathbb{C}[u] when ri=0r_{i}=0; Prop 9.1 and Thm 9.2 are unchanged, the summands of μ\mu indexed by ri=0r_{i}=0 being zero. Only Lem 9.3 needs amending: Bi​(O)=0B_{i}(O)=0 is available for those ii with ri>0r_{i}>0, which is all that its proof uses, and the conclusions Λ⁡(O)≠0\Lambda(O)\neq 0 and Jacu⁡(B2,…,Bn)​(O)=κ/Λ⁡(O)\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,B_{n})(O)=\kappa/\Lambda(O) persist.

Proposition 10.3.

Let 𝐰=(1,−r2,…,−rn)\mathbf{w}=(1,-r_{2},\dots,-r_{n}) with ri≥0r_{i}\geq 0 and m=∑i≥2rim=\sum_{i\geq 2}r_{i}. If m≥2m\geq 2, then Thm 9.4 holds verbatim: a solution of Eq. 12 with Λ∉ℂ\Lambda\notin\mathbb{C} is a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, and the family is parametrised by the scheme 𝒴𝐫,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}} of Sec. 9. If m=1m=1, that is if 𝐰=(1,−1,0,…,0)\mathbf{w}=(1,-1,0,\dots,0), the exponent m−1m-1 vanishes, detJ​G=±Jacu⁡(P2,…,Pn)\det JG=\pm\Jac_{u}(P_{2},\dots,P_{n}), and the Keller condition for GG is exactly the Keller condition for G¯\overline{G} in dimension n−1n-1, with no contracted locus, as in Rem 3.3.

So the parabolic case is not a separate difficulty: with an elliptic nonzero part it is the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension zz, and with a hyperbolic nonzero part of the above type it is the theory of Sec. 9. What is left open is the parabolic case whose hyperbolic part falls outside that type, and that is the same restriction we meet next.

10.4. Third cut: the shape of the hyperbolic quotient

Let 𝐰\mathbf{w} be hyperbolic, and let n+n_{+} be the number of positive weights. Replacing 𝐰\mathbf{w} by −𝐰-\mathbf{w} if necessary, assume n+≤n−n+n_{+}\leq n-n_{+}. For n=3n=3 this forces n+=1n_{+}=1: the case of two positive weights, such as 𝐰=(1,1,−1)\mathbf{w}=(1,1,-1), is carried by the substitution t↦t−1t\mapsto t^{-1} and a coordinate permutation to 𝐰=(1,−1,−1)\mathbf{w}=(1,-1,-1), which is the type Eq. 13 with (r,s)=(1,1)(r,s)=(1,1) and is treated below. The first genuinely new configuration with n+≥2n_{+}\geq 2 therefore occurs in dimension four.

The construction of Sec. 8 and Sec. 9 requires n+=1n_{+}=1 and the positive weight equal to 11. The two hypotheses fail for different reasons.

If n+=1n_{+}=1 with positive weight w1=a≥2w_{1}=a\geq 2, the invariant ring is generated by the monomials xc​y𝐛x^{c}y^{\mathbf{b}} with c​a=∑iri​bica=\sum_{i}r_{i}b_{i}, where 𝐰=(a,−r2,…,−rn)\mathbf{w}=(a,-r_{2},\dots,-r_{n}), and this semigroup need not be free. Already 𝐰=(2,−1,−1)\mathbf{w}=(2,-1,-1) gives ℂ⁡[x​y2,x​y​z,x​z2]\mathbb{C}[xy^{2},xyz,xz^{2}], a quadric cone, as noted in Rem 8.4: the reduction then takes place on a singular quotient, where Jacu\Jac_{u} has no elementary meaning and the graded pieces are modules over a non-polynomial ring rather than monomial ideals.

If n+≥2n_{+}\geq 2, so n≥4n\geq 4, the weight-11 piece is no longer generated by a single element over the invariants. For 𝐰=(1,1,−r3,−r4)\mathbf{w}=(1,1,-r_{3},-r_{4}) it is x1​R+x2​Rx_{1}R+x_{2}R with RR the invariant ring, since a monomial of weight 11 is divisible by x1x_{1} or by x2x_{2} but need not be divisible by a prescribed one. The description Eq. 11, and with it the single factor Λ\Lambda and the contracted locus {Λ=0}\{\Lambda=0\} around which Sec. 8 is organised, has no analogue. The quotient is in general singular here as well: for 𝐰=(1,1,−1,−1)\mathbf{w}=(1,1,-1,-1) the invariant ring is the affine cone over ℙ1×ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}.

We therefore restrict to

(13) 𝐰=(1,−r2,…,−rn),ri>0,𝐪=𝐰,\mathbf{w}=(1,-r_{2},\dots,-r_{n}),\qquad r_{i}>0,\qquad\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{w},

the setting of Sec. 9, and record the two omitted configurations as open. Within the hyperbolic case the classification is thus governed by more than the signature: by the number of positive weights, and by the value of the positive one.

10.5. The two ends of the filtration

Fix a type Eq. 13. Two constraints on a point of 𝒴𝐫,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}} are visible without any computation, one at the top of the degree filtration and one at the bottom. We record both, since the emptiness proofs below use them together.

For the top, fix 𝐝=(d2,…,dn,dΛ)\mathbf{d}=(d_{2},\dots,d_{n},d_{\Lambda}) and write 𝒴𝐫,𝐝=⊆𝒴𝐫,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{=}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}} for the locally closed subscheme of points whose data has these degrees exactly, so that

𝒴𝐫,𝐝∘=⨆𝐝′≤𝐝,dΛ′≥1𝒴𝐫,𝐝′=.\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}}=\bigsqcup_{\mathbf{d}^{\prime}\leq\mathbf{d},\ d^{\prime}_{\Lambda}\geq 1}\mathcal{Y}^{=}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}^{\prime}}.

D=dΛ+∑i≥2di−(n−1).D=d_{\Lambda}+\sum_{i\geq 2}d_{i}-(n-1).

Let [G]∈𝒴𝐫,𝐝=[G]\in\mathcal{Y}^{=}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}}. Then μ\mu has degree at most DD, and its degree-DD component is μ⁡(B^2,…,B^n,Λ^)\mu(\hat{B}_{2},\dots,\hat{B}_{n},\hat{\Lambda}). Since D≥1D\geq 1, the Keller condition Eq. 12 forces

that is, the n−1n-1 forms B^i​Λ^ri\hat{B}_{i}\hat{\Lambda}^{r_{i}} are algebraically dependent over ℂ\mathbb{C}.

The summand Λ​Jacu​(B2,…,Bn)\Lambda\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,B_{n}) has degree at most dΛ+∑i(di−1)=Dd_{\Lambda}+\sum_{i}(d_{i}-1)=D, and the summand ri​Bi​Jacu​(B2,…,Λ,…,Bn)r_{i}B_{i}\Jac_{u}(B_{2},\dots,\Lambda,\dots,B_{n}) has degree at most

di+(dΛ−1)+∑j≠i(dj−1)=D,d_{i}+(d_{\Lambda}-1)+\sum_{j\neq i}(d_{j}-1)=D,

and in each the degree-DD part is obtained by replacing every argument by its leading form. Hence the degree-DD component of μ\mu is μ⁡(B^2,…,B^n,Λ^)\mu(\hat{B}_{2},\dots,\hat{B}_{n},\hat{\Lambda}). Since deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1 and each BiB_{i} lies in the maximal ideal, D≥1D\geq 1, while μ=κ\mu=\kappa has degree 00; so that component vanishes. Applying Thm 9.2 to the forms gives

μ⁡(B^2,…,B^n,Λ^)=Λ^−(m−1)​Jacu​(B^2​Λ^r2,…,B^n​Λ^rn),\mu(\hat{B}_{2},\dots,\hat{B}_{n},\hat{\Lambda})=\hat{\Lambda}^{-(m-1)}\Jac_{u}\bigl(\hat{B}_{2}\hat{\Lambda}^{r_{2}},\dots,\hat{B}_{n}\hat{\Lambda}^{r_{n}}\bigr),

and the last assertion is the Jacobian criterion for algebraic dependence in characteristic zero. ∎

For the bottom of the filtration, write Bˇi\check{B}_{i} for the initial form of BiB_{i} at OO.

Lemma 10.5.

Let [G]∈𝒴𝐫,𝐝∘[G]\in\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}}. Then each BiB_{i} has order exactly 11 at OO, the linear forms Bˇ2,…,Bˇn\check{B}_{2},\dots,\check{B}_{n} are linearly independent, and

For n=3n=3 the forms are binary and Thm 10.4 becomes explicit. Write (r2,r3)=(r,s)(r_{2},r_{3})=(r,s), B2=BB_{2}=B, B3=AB_{3}=A and 𝐝=(d1,d2,d3)\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}) as in Sec. 8, and set

Theorem 10.6.

Let [G]∈𝒴r,s,𝐝=[G]\in\mathcal{Y}^{=}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}, and let A^,B^,Λ^\hat{A},\hat{B},\hat{\Lambda} be the leading forms, of degrees d1,d2,d3d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}. Then there are a binary form hh of degree ee and constants κ1,κ2∈ℂ×\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2}\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} with

(14) βi+r​γi=νBe​mi,αi+s​γi=νAe​mi,\beta_{i}+r\gamma_{i}=\tfrac{\nu_{B}}{e}\,m_{i},\qquad\alpha_{i}+s\gamma_{i}=\tfrac{\nu_{A}}{e}\,m_{i},

together with ∑iαi=d1\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}=d_{1}, ∑iβi=d2\sum_{i}\beta_{i}=d_{2}, ∑iγi=d3\sum_{i}\gamma_{i}=d_{3}, ∑imi=e\sum_{i}m_{i}=e.

Proof.

Put f=B^​Λ^rf=\hat{B}\hat{\Lambda}^{r} and g=A^​Λ^sg=\hat{A}\hat{\Lambda}^{s}, nonzero forms of degrees νB\nu_{B} and νA\nu_{A}, satisfying {f,g}=0\{f,g\}=0 by Thm 10.4. Hence fνA=c​gνBf^{\nu_{A}}=cg^{\nu_{B}} for some c∈ℂ×c\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}.

Over ℂ\mathbb{C} both forms split. Let ℓ1,…,ℓk\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{k} be the distinct linear factors occurring in ff or in gg, with multiplicities φi\varphi_{i} in ff and γi′\gamma^{\prime}_{i} in gg. With h=∏ℓimih=\prod\ell_{i}^{m_{i}} we get f=κ1​hνB′f=\kappa_{1}h^{\nu_{B}^{\prime}} and g=κ2​hνA′g=\kappa_{2}h^{\nu_{A}^{\prime}}. The system Eq. 14 is the equality of multiplicities at ℓi\ell_{i} in these two identities, and the four sums record the degrees. ∎

If e=1e=1, then every point of 𝒴r,s,𝐝=\mathcal{Y}^{=}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} has k=1k=1: the three leading forms are powers of a single linear form.

k≤∑imi=ek\leq\sum_{i}m_{i}=e. ∎

Remark 10.8.

Thm 10.6 is a stratification of the leading data, not by itself an emptiness criterion. Indeed Eq. 14 always admits the solution k=1k=1, m=(e)m=(e), γ=(d3)\gamma=(d_{3}), for which β1=νB−r​d3=d2\beta_{1}=\nu_{B}-rd_{3}=d_{2} and α1=νA−s​d3=d1\alpha_{1}=\nu_{A}-sd_{3}=d_{1} and the inequalities of Eq. 15 reduce to d1,d2≥0d_{1},d_{2}\geq 0. Emptiness must therefore be proved stratum by stratum, by combining Thm 10.6 with Lem 10.5 or with the linear algebra of Prop 8.12. Both routes are taken below.

Example 10.9.

The next result is the first place where the two ends of the filtration are used together. It supersedes the computation of Rem 10.11 below, which treated (r,s)=(1,1)(r,s)=(1,1) only.

Theorem 10.10.

Let r,s>0r,s>0 and d3≥1d_{3}\geq 1. Then 𝒴r,s,(1,1,d3)∘=∅\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,(1,1,d_{3})}=\emptyset. Equivalently, no graded Keller counterexample of type Eq. 13 in dimension three has both AA and BB of degree one in the invariants.

For (r,s)=(1,1)(r,s)=(1,1) the conclusion can be seen directly, and the computation exhibits an operator worth recording. Write A=a1​u+a2​vA=a_{1}u+a_{2}v, B=b1​u+b2​vB=b_{1}u+b_{2}v and δ=b1​a2−b2​a1\delta=b_{1}a_{2}-b_{2}a_{1}. By Thm 10.10 the smallest cases left open in dimension three are (r,s)=(1,1)(r,s)=(1,1) with 𝐝=(2,1,d3)\mathbf{d}=(2,1,d_{3}) and 𝐝=(1,2,d3)\mathbf{d}=(1,2,d_{3}); whether 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−1,−1))\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-1,-1)) is empty we do not know.

10.8. Constructing counterexamples

Thm 10.6 turns the construction of a graded counterexample of given exact degrees into three steps, the first finite and the third linear. We describe them, and then carry them out at the degrees of Eq. 1.

Step 1: the integer enumeration. Fix (r,s)(r,s) and 𝐝=(d1,d2,d3)\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}), and let νA,νB,e\nu_{A},\nu_{B},e be as above. Summing the two families in Eq. 14 over ii gives ∑iβi=νB−r​d3=d2\sum_{i}\beta_{i}=\nu_{B}-rd_{3}=d_{2} and ∑iαi=νA−s​d3=d1\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}=\nu_{A}-sd_{3}=d_{1}, so the degree conditions on α\alpha and β\beta hold automatically. The data to be enumerated is only the pair (m,γ)(m,\gamma), and Eq. 14 reduces to

(15) ∑imi=e,∑iγi=d3,νBe​mi≥r​γi,νAe​mi≥s​γi,\sum_{i}m_{i}=e,\qquad\sum_{i}\gamma_{i}=d_{3},\qquad\tfrac{\nu_{B}}{e}m_{i}\geq r\gamma_{i},\qquad\tfrac{\nu_{A}}{e}m_{i}\geq s\gamma_{i},

in nonnegative integers, with αi=νAe​mi−s​γi\alpha_{i}=\tfrac{\nu_{A}}{e}m_{i}-s\gamma_{i} and βi=νBe​mi−r​γi\beta_{i}=\tfrac{\nu_{B}}{e}m_{i}-r\gamma_{i}. If mi=0m_{i}=0 then βi=−r​γi≥0\beta_{i}=-r\gamma_{i}\geq 0 forces γi=0\gamma_{i}=0 and hence αi=βi=0\alpha_{i}=\beta_{i}=0, so ℓi\ell_{i} does not occur; we may assume mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1, whence 1≤k≤e1\leq k\leq e. The enumeration is over compositions of ee into kk positive parts and of d3d_{3} into kk nonnegative parts, a finite list, and it produces a finite set of strata covering 𝒴r,s,𝐝=\mathcal{Y}^{=}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}. By Rem 10.8 the list is never empty, so this step does not by itself decide emptiness; what it does is replace one search by finitely many much smaller ones.

Step 2: normalising the leading forms. A solution of Eq. 15 determines A^,B^,Λ^\hat{A},\hat{B},\hat{\Lambda} up to the choice of the kk pairwise non-proportional linear forms ℓi\ell_{i} and of scalars. The scalars are absorbed by the 𝔾m3\mathbb{G}_{m}^{3}-action of Thm 8.9. The linear forms are acted on by the linear part of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, which depends on (r,s)(r,s): the degree-one part of VAV_{A} is ℂ​v\mathbb{C}v when r<sr<s and ℂ​u+ℂ​v\mathbb{C}u+\mathbb{C}v when r≥sr\geq s, and that of VBV_{B} is ℂ​u\mathbb{C}u when r>sr>s and ℂ​u+ℂ​v\mathbb{C}u+\mathbb{C}v when r≤sr\leq s. Hence the linear part of 𝒢\mathcal{G} is

GL2⁡ if ​r=s,a Borel subgroup of ​GL2​ if ​r≠s.\GL_{2}\ \text{ if }r=s,\qquad\text{a Borel subgroup of }\GL_{2}\ \text{ if }r\neq s.

Modulo scalars this is PGL2\mathrm{PGL}_{2}, acting with finitely many orbits on configurations of k≤3k\leq 3 points of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, respectively the affine group 𝔸1⋊𝔾m\mathbb{A}^{1}\rtimes\mathbb{G}_{m}, acting with finitely many orbits on configurations of k≤2k\leq 2 points. So the leading data carries no continuous modulus when k≤3k\leq 3 (case r=sr=s) or k≤2k\leq 2 (case r≠sr\neq s).

Step 3: the lower-order terms. With the leading forms fixed, what remains is to solve Eq. 10 for the lower-order coefficients of AA, BB and Λ\Lambda. This is the situation of Prop 8.12: fixing BB and Λ\Lambda, the equation is linear in AA, and a solution with κ≠0\kappa\neq 0 exists exactly when

rank⁡TB,Λ=rank⁡(π∘TB,Λ)+1.\rank T_{B,\Lambda}=\rank(\pi\circ T_{B,\Lambda})+1.

The search space is much smaller than the ambient ℙ⁡(VB​(𝐝))×ℙ⁡(VΛ​(𝐝))\mathbb{P}(V_{B}(\mathbf{d}))\times\mathbb{P}(V_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{d})) of Sec. 8, since the leading coefficients of BB and Λ\Lambda are prescribed by Step 1 and normalised by Step 2.

The scheme 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} is defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, so Steps 1–3 may be carried out over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. Here some care is needed: a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-point of 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}} spreads out to a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-section of 𝒴r,s,𝐝\mathcal{Y}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}, but the open conditions μ00≠0\mu_{00}\neq 0 and deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1 may fail on reduction, and the primes at which they fail depend on the point. So 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘​(𝔽p)=∅\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}(\mathbb{F}_{p})=\emptyset for a single pp does not prove 𝒴r,s,𝐝∘​(ℚ)=∅\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{r,s,\mathbf{d}}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset; what it proves is that every ℚ\mathbb{Q}-point degenerates at pp. Emptiness over ℚ\mathbb{Q} follows only from emptiness over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} for all pp outside an effectively bounded set, or from emptiness over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, for which the elimination over algebraically closed fields recorded in Sec. 8 applies.

Remark 10.14.

Prop 10.13 concerns the exact-degree stratum, which is where [F][F] lives. The bounded scheme 𝒴1,2,(4,3,1)∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1)} also contains the strata 𝒴1,2,(d1′,d2′,1)=\mathcal{Y}^{=}_{1,2,(d_{1}^{\prime},d_{2}^{\prime},1)} with d1′≤4d_{1}^{\prime}\leq 4, d2′≤3d_{2}^{\prime}\leq 3; of these, (d1′,d2′)=(1,1)(d_{1}^{\prime},d_{2}^{\prime})=(1,1) is empty by Thm 10.10, and the remaining ten are not settled here. The two contradictions in the proof above both read “deg⁡β0=3\deg\beta_{0}=3 while deg⁡α1≤2\deg\alpha_{1}\leq 2”, so they use the exact degrees essentially and do not transfer.

10.9. Summary

For the fourth row the family is the set of rational points of the explicit scheme 𝒴𝐫,𝐝∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{d}} of Sec. 9; its leading stratum is constrained by Thm 10.4, in dimension three by the system Eq. 14, and its initial stratum by Lem 10.5. The map Eq. 1 is one of its points, and whether it is the only one, up to 𝒢\mathcal{G}, is Rem 8.13. Three facts frame that question at the degrees of Eq. 1: the leading configuration is forced to be that of Eq. 1 (Prop 10.13), the leading data carries no continuous modulus (Example 10.12), and a family with varying leading data would require e≥3e\geq 3. None of these excludes a family with constant leading data, which is what Prop 8.12 would have to decide.

Finally, the parameter space itself is of the opposite signature to the map it parametrises. By Prop 8.14 the triples (A,B,Λ)(A,B,\Lambda) modulo the natural 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} form a weighted projective space 𝕎​ℙ​(𝝎)\mathbb{WP}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) with all weights positive, so the arithmetic of a hyperbolic counterexample is governed by an elliptic moduli space, of exactly the type studied in [11]. This is the sharpest form of the comparison announced in the introduction, and it is the reason the counting function of Prop 8.14 is well posed.

11. Concluding remarks

The results above leave a picture with some proved edges and some open middle. We close by recording both: why the mechanism of Eq. 1 needs dimension three, where the classification of Sec. 10 actually stops, what a counting theory over ℚ\mathbb{Q} would require, and how the two papers’ settings fit together.

Why dimension three

For a weight type Eq. 13 the Keller condition is, by Prop 9.1, the single divisorial identity

(20) Jacu⁡(P2,…,Pn)=κ​Λm−1,m=∑i≥2ri:\Jac_{u}(P_{2},\dots,P_{n})=\kappa\,\Lambda^{\,m-1},\qquad m=\sum_{i\geq 2}r_{i}:

the Jacobian of the quotient map vanishes along the contracted locus {Λ=0}\{\Lambda=0\}, to the order prescribed by the weights, and nowhere else. In dimension two this is an identity between polynomials in one variable, and there Jacu\Jac_{u} is a derivative: with G¯=B​Λr\overline{G}=B\Lambda^{r} one has Jacu⁡(P)=G¯′\Jac_{u}(P)=\overline{G}^{\prime}, so Eq. 20 reads G¯′=κ​Λr−1\overline{G}^{\prime}=\kappa\Lambda^{r-1}. Comparing degrees, deg⁡B+r​deg⁡Λ−1=(r−1)​deg⁡Λ\deg B+r\deg\Lambda-1=(r-1)\deg\Lambda, that is deg⁡B+deg⁡Λ=1\deg B+\deg\Lambda=1, which is impossible since BB lies in the maximal ideal and deg⁡Λ≥1\deg\Lambda\geq 1. This is the argument of Thm 3.4 in the coordinates of Sec. 9, and it closes the case because the degree of a derivative drops by exactly one: a curve admits an exact ramification count, and the count leaves no room.

In dimension three and above no such accounting holds. The quotient is a surface, Jacu,v\Jac_{u,v} is not a derivative, and the discrepancy that the degree count would have to absorb is absorbed instead by the geometry: the quotient map is not proper, and over a general point of the discriminant the missing sheets escape to infinity rather than coming together (Prop 5.1). The mechanism behind Eq. 1 needs somewhere for ramification to go, and a curve has nowhere. Consistently with this, Rem 3.3 and Prop 10.3 show that it is the contracted locus, and not the hyperbolic signature, that makes a counterexample possible: when Λ\Lambda is constant, Eq. 20 degenerates to the Keller condition for G¯\overline{G} and the graded problem in dimension nn becomes the ordinary Jacobian Conjecture in dimension n−1n-1.

This also suggests where to look for structure we have not examined: the two GIT manifestations of the hyperbolic action, of which we have used only {x≠0}\{x\neq 0\}, and whose other chamber appears related to the weighted projective line ℙ⁡(1,2)\mathbb{P}(1,2); we have not pursued this.

Where the classification stops

Table 1 records what the signature decides and what it does not. The elliptic case is empty in every dimension (Thm 3.1), dimension two is empty for every signature (Thm 3.4), and the parabolic case is not a third phenomenon but a degeneration of the other two: with elliptic nonzero part it is the Jacobian Conjecture in the number of vanishing weights (Thm 10.2), and with hyperbolic nonzero part of the type Eq. 13 it is the theory of Sec. 9 verbatim (Prop 10.3). What survives is a genuinely finer invariant than the signature: within the hyperbolic case the reduction to Eq. 20 requires that the weight-one graded piece be free of rank one over the invariants, which holds exactly when there is a single positive weight and it equals 11. Both failures are real. With one positive weight a≥2a\geq 2 the invariant ring is not polynomial — already 𝐰=(2,−1,−1)\mathbf{w}=(2,-1,-1) gives a quadric cone — and Jacu\Jac_{u} loses its elementary meaning; with n+≥2n_{+}\geq 2, first possible in dimension four, the weight-one piece is generated by two elements and the factor Λ\Lambda has no analogue.

Four questions are left, in increasing order of how much we expect them to require.

  1. (1)

    Is 𝒴1,2,(4,3,1)∘\mathcal{Y}^{\circ}_{1,2,(4,3,1)} a single 𝒢\mathcal{G}-orbit (Rem 8.13)? At these degrees Prop 10.13 forces the leading configuration of Eq. 1 and Example 10.12 shows the leading data carries no continuous modulus, so what remains is the linear algebra of Prop 8.12: a rank condition on a 13×2813\times 28 matrix over an eleven-dimensional base. This is a computation, not a theorem, and we regard it as the first thing to do.

  2. (2)

    Is 𝒦⁡(3,(1,−1,−1))\mathcal{K}(3,(1,-1,-1)) empty? By Thm 10.10 the smallest undecided degrees are 𝐝=(2,1,d3)\mathbf{d}=(2,1,d_{3}) and 𝐝=(1,2,d3)\mathbf{d}=(1,2,d_{3}), and the same three-step search applies.

  3. (3)

    Does Prop 10.13 hold uniformly? Its proof — normalise ℓ\ell, expand in the transverse variable, extract the top coefficient, integrate the resulting logarithmic identity, compare degrees — appears not to use the particular degrees except at the last step. A statement that the stratum k=1k=1 is empty for every (r,s,𝐝)(r,s,\mathbf{d}) would restore the content that Cor 10.7 does not have.

  4. (4)

    The two omitted hyperbolic shapes: positive weight ≥2\geq 2, where the quotient is singular, and n+≥2n_{+}\geq 2, where it is smooth but the description Eq. 11 fails. These need different methods, and the second is the first place where dimension four is not a formality.

Arithmetic

Restricting Eq. 1 to {x=0}\{x=0\} gives (y,z)↦(z+4​y2,y, 0)(y,z)\mapsto(z+4y^{2},\,y,\,0), a Jonquières automorphism of the plane onto {c=0}\{c=0\}, so every rational point of {c=0}\{c=0\} lifts. In the counting function

Z(X)=#{(a,b,c)∈ℚ3:H≤X,F−1(a,b,c)∩ℚ3≠∅}Z(X)=\#\{(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{Q}^{3}:H\leq X,\ F^{-1}(a,b,c)\cap\mathbb{Q}^{3}\neq\emptyset\}

this stratum should dominate, much as coordinate strata dominate the counting problems of [11], while off the stratum the count is governed by the splitting of Eq. 7; one expects the exponent there to come from a linear program, as in the positive-weight setting, though we have proved nothing in this direction. Part of the difficulty is foundational: the weighted heights of [2, 11] require positive weights, the stacky height frameworks require properness, and Eq. 1 lives where both hypotheses fail. A height theory for hyperbolic quotients — a quotient height coupled with an orbit term — would let the problem be posed precisely, and seems to us the natural first step.

The contrast with the parameter space is worth stating plainly, because it is the one place where the two settings meet inside a single object. By Prop 8.14 the triples (A,B,Λ)(A,B,\Lambda) modulo the natural 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} form a weighted projective space with all weights positive. The counting function 𝒩⁡(X)\mathcal{N}(X) on it is therefore well posed, by the very theory of [2, 11] that Z⁡(X)Z(X) falls outside: a hyperbolic counterexample is parametrised by an elliptic moduli space. Whether 𝒩⁡(X)\mathcal{N}(X) measures anything beyond the growth of a single orbit is Rem 8.13 again.

One classification

The settings of [11] and of this note are two manifestations of one classification. For a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action the governing invariant is the position of 00 relative to the weights. All weights of one sign, the elliptic case, gives proper, finite, ramified quotient maps, where the obstruction to lifting a rational point is a Kummer condition [11]; 00 strictly between the weights, the hyperbolic case, gives non-proper quotients with contracted loci, where liftability is the splitting of a resolvent, in this example with nonabelian Galois group and thin image; and a zero weight interpolates, contributing a cylinder factor which, as Thm 10.2 shows, carries the whole difficulty. In dimensions two and three every algebraic 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-action on affine space is linearizable [5, 6], so there the classification covers all actions.

The Jacobian problem is trivial in the elliptic case (Thm 3.1) and in dimension two for every signature (Thm 3.4), and the two facts have different proofs but the same source: in both, properness or an exact degree count forecloses the loss of a sheet. What is striking is that the dichotomy is not clean on the arithmetic side. Rem 5.3 exhibits a Kummer condition inside the hyperbolic example, on the line where the stabilizer is μ2\mu_{2}, and Rem 8.15 suggests another at the level of moduli; the abelian obstruction of the positive-weight theory returns wherever the stabilizer is nontrivial. This points to a stratification by stabilizer type, refining the trichotomy rather than being refined by it, and it is the shape we would expect a general theory to take: a theory of lifting rational points along equivariant maps, organized by signature and by stabilizer, of which [11] is the elliptic case and the analysis above a first hyperbolic example.

For a torus of higher rank the geometric side is classical — the invariant becomes the position of the origin relative to the convex hull of the weights, and the manifestations form the GIT fan — so the arithmetic questions can at least be asked in that generality. We hope to return to this.
